data:
CVA6 is designed to be developed with automation, not only by hand. The
AGENTS-*.md files and the build-platform/ command surface are the two main
mechanisms that make the repository legible to an LLM agent.The rise of large language models has changed the economics of documentation.
Manuals that once served only human readers now serve as retrieval corpora for
automated agents. This dual readership imposes a new quality bar: the text must
be precise enough for a human to understand and structured enough for an agent
to execute. CVA6 meets this bar by encoding the expert's navigation path into
the AGENTS-*.md files and the g6lc-build command surface. An agent that
follows this path is not guessing; it is replaying the reasoning that an
experienced engineer would perform.
data.the-agent-loop#The agent loop:
A typical AI-led workflow looks like this:
Receive intent. "Add L2 cache support to CVA6."
Resolve to a guide. Open AGENTS.md and find the intent in the
navigation table → agents/guides/AGENTS-l2l3-cache.md.
Load spec context. Read the relevant agents/spec/*.html summaries
(memory model, PMA, Zic64b, CMOs).
Locate code seam. The guide lists primary code loci (e.g.
core/cache_subsystem/, core/cva6.sv:1400-1560).
Plan changes. Extend cva6_cfg_t in core/include/config_pkg.sv, add a
config package, gate the new logic, and add tests.
Run build platform. g6lc-build resolves config, discovers sources,
preflights tools, and runs the chosen test suite.
Verify and document. Update traceability files, DFT hooks, PMU events,
and docs.
This loop is the same closed-loop engineering process used in safety-critical
and high-reliability projects, but automated. The intent is the requirement;
the guide is the design document; the code loci are the implementation; and the
build platform is the integration and verification harness. The key insight is
that the agent never needs to "understand" the whole design at once. It only
needs to understand the next hop in the graph, which is exactly how human
experts navigate large systems.
data.the-agents--contract#The AGENTS-* contra:
Each AGENTS-*.md file follows a similar contract:
What it is for. One or two sentences of intent.
Spec anchors. Canonical specs/riscv-spec.html#anchor references.
Code loci. path/to/file.sv:start-end references.
Seam. Where the change should be made (CVXIF, AXI adapter, config struct,
board JSON, PDK drop-in).
Checklist. The SoC-readiness items that must be true before the change is
done (synth, config, verif, DFT, backend, docs).
Because the guides are small, single-topic files, an LLM can load only the 3–6
files relevant to the prompt instead of the whole repository.The contract format is itself a form of interface design. By standardizing on
intent, spec anchors, code loci, seams, and checklists, the repository creates
a predictable API for reasoning. A human reviewer can quickly confirm that an
agent loaded the right documents; an automated tool can parse the file list and
checklist and execute the corresponding commands. This predictability is what
makes the agent workflow trustworthy enough to be part of a real engineering
process.

data.build-platform-as-the-agent-executor#Bui:
The g6lc-build command is the executor for the agent's plan. It:
Reads .config.ts and resolves the whole SoC state.
Provisions or skips tools based on what is missing.
Runs regression suites and reports preflight skips (missing tool, missing
submodule, missing UVM).
Generates board packages, vendor sync reports, and technology readiness
reports.
Because the platform is typed and deterministic, an agent can call it
programmatically and trust the exit code and JSON output.The build platform's role as executor is what separates a useful agent from a
dangerous one. An LLM that edits source files directly can introduce subtle
bugs across the whole tree; an LLM that delegates execution to g6lc-build
operates through a typed, tested, and preflighted harness. Preflight checks
are especially important: they prevent the agent from failing because of a
missing tool or submodule, and they report skip reasons so the user knows what
to install. This is the same discipline used in cloud build systems, where
hermetic execution is a prerequisite for trustworthy automation.
data.grok-build--devin-style-development#grok:
A "grok-build" or Devin-style agent pass over CVA6 is conceptually:
plan  = read(AGENTS.md) → read(relevant AGENTS-*.md) → read(spec) → plan(changes)
build = g6lc-build <command> --dry-run
edit  = gated RTL / config / board / vendor / technology
verify = g6lc-build test --<group>
doc   = update AGENTS-*.md + this docs site
The key is that planning happens against the guides, while execution
happens through g6lc-build. The guides supply the "what" and the "where";
the platform supplies the "how" and the "did it pass."A "grok-build" pass is not a one-shot prompt; it is an iterative collaboration
between a planner and an executor. The planner reads the knowledge graph and
proposes a change; the executor validates the environment and runs the
relevant command; the planner interprets the output and decides the next step.
This separation of concerns mirrors the division between architecture and
implementation in industrial teams: one group decides what should change,
another group validates that it can be built and tested.
data.adding-a-new-ai-readable-guide#Adding a:
When a new feature domain appears (for example, a new accelerator interface),
create:
agents/guides/AGENTS-<domain>.md — the feature playbook.
The relevant agents/spec/*.html sub-files for spec anchors.
A page under docs/website/pages/ (e.g. architecture/<domain>.mdx) that
links the guide to the high-level narrative.
An entry in AGENTS-todo.md if it is a tracked phase.
This keeps the knowledge graph navigable by both humans and LLMs.

data:
CVA6 is organized as a set of concentric layers that take a RISC-V CPU core
to a finished SoC product:
RISC-V CPU core (core/)
    ⇄ on-die uncore / FPGA emulation platform (corev_apu/)
        ⇄ motherboard / board layer (corev-mb/)
            ⇄ foundry / process technology (pd/pdk/)
                ⇄ vendor controllers & PHY (vendor/, corev_apu/)
                    ⇄ build automation & AI orchestration (build-platform/)
                         ⇄ structural timing package (sv-timing/)  [spawn only]
Each silicon layer has its own directory, config gate, and agent guide. The
build platform is the spine: it reads the repo-root .config.ts and drives
setup, simulation, board selection, vendor sync, technology checks, and the
optional timings host adapter. sv-timing/ is not a silicon layer; it
is an independent analysis package that the spine may spawn (see
sv-timing).This layered model is not an accident of history; it is the physical design of
a reusable silicon IP business. A CPU core that can be sold or reused across
multiple SoCs must remain agnostic to the boards and processes that surround it.
An uncore layer must be able to change controllers without rewriting the core.
A board layer must be able to target a new physical platform without forking
the RTL. And a technology layer must be able to bind a foundry process without
contaminating the generic source. Each arrow in the diagram above represents a
one-way dependency that protects the inner layer from the outer layer's
concerns, which is the same dependency discipline used in commercial IP
ecosystems such as Arm Flexible Access, SiFive Core Complex, and the OpenHW
Group's own portfolio.
data.why-this-structure-exists#Why this struc:
CVA6 is not a software model; it is silicon IP that is integrated into SoCs,
booted into Linux, and taped out. The directory layout is therefore designed to
keep ** concerns separated**:
core/ has no dependency on corev_apu/ — it can be simulated and
synthesized stand-alone.
corev_apu/ depends on core/ and adds the FPGA/uncore platform.
corev-mb/ describes the board around the die without editing core/ or
corev_apu/src/.
vendor/ holds third-party IP that is fetched and scanned on demand.
build-platform/ automates the cross-platform setup and orchestration.
sv-timing/ is a standalone structural-timing package (optional host:
g6lc-build timings).
architecture/ holds non-compiled extension scaffolds and pointers to
live upgrade status (OoO, SMT, L2, …) without entering flists.
agents/ and AGENTS-*.md contain the living guides that agents and
humans use to navigate each layer.
The AGENTS-*.md layer is the key to scaling this repository. As the project
grows, the number of files, spec subchapters, and verification suites grows
faster than any single engineer can memorize. The agent guides compress that
complexity into a curated retrieval graph, so that both human and automated
readers can resolve intent to a small set of relevant documents. This is the
same knowledge-management pattern used in large-scale software monorepos, but
adapted to the unique needs of hardware: precise file-line references, spec
anchors, and silicon sign-off checklists.
data.key-design-rules#Key design rules:
Config is the single source of truth. The cva6_cfg_t struct in
core/include/config_pkg.sv gates CPU features; the repo-root .config.ts
gates the whole SoC build.
Add at a sanctioned seam. New compute prefers the CVXIF coprocessor
boundary; new memories go through tc_sram; new board targets go under
corev-mb/architecture/; new PDK drop-ins go under pd/pdk/.
Never churn the working hierarchy. New features are additive; they do not
move existing files or break flists.
Every change is verified in lockstep. RTL, tests, formal properties,
DFT hooks, and docs are updated together.
Each rule addresses a specific failure mode seen in industrial SoC projects.
"Config as the single source of truth" prevents silent divergence between the
RTL and the build scripts that invoke it. "Add at a sanctioned seam" prevents
ad hoc coupling that later makes timing closure or floorplanning impossible.
"Never churn the working hierarchy" preserves the investment that partners and
tool flows have made in the existing directory structure and flists. "Every
change is verified in lockstep" closes the gap between "it simulates" and "it
is ready for silicon," where DFT, formal equivalence, and documentation are
traditionally left as afterthoughts.

Three documents form the cross-cutting contract for every ISA-visible or
SoC-visible change: the RISC-V specification, the CVA6 device tree, and the
AGENTS-*.md architecture guides. Keeping them aligned is what makes a feature
"real" for software bring-up.Traceability is the discipline that turns a collection of source files into an
auditable engineering artifact. In safety-critical and security-critical
markets, traceability is often a contractual requirement: every feature must be
traceable to a requirement, every requirement to an implementation, and every
implementation to a verification method. CVA6 adopts this discipline not as
bureaucracy, but as a correctness mechanism. When the RISC-V spec, the device
tree, and the agent guides are kept aligned, the project can answer the
question "does this change break the SoC contract?" before silicon is wasted.
data.1-risc-v-specification-of-record#1. RISC:
The file specs/riscv-spec.html is the canonical spec of record. It is
organized into three volumes:
I Unprivileged ISA — instruction encodings, base integer, extensions.
II Privileged ISA — CSRs, privilege modes, interrupts, virtual memory.
III Profiles — platform profiles and optionality.
The agents/spec/ directory contains one small summary file per subchapter
(riscv-spec-<Vol>-<X.y>-<slug>.html). These summaries give the canonical
anchor, a Logisplain prose summary, pseudo-SystemVerilog synthesis notes, and a
CVA6 status line.Having the full ISA manual in the repository is not just a convenience; it is a
form of configuration management. External spec URLs rot, versions drift, and
different engineers silently reference different snapshots. By pinning the
spec as a single file (specs/riscv-spec.html) and producing per-subchapter
summaries in agents/spec/, CVA6 ensures that every ISA-visible change is
argued against the same normative text. The sub-files also serve as a
negotiation boundary: an engineer can propose a change by updating the relevant
agents/spec/ summary, and reviewers can evaluate whether the summary
accurately reflects the canonical anchor.
data.traceability-files#Traceability files:
Three root files are updated whenever ISA-visible code or tests change:
AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md — RISC-V chapter ⇄ CVA6 RTL.
AGENTS-specs-to-tests.md — RISC-V chapter ⇄ test suite.
AGENTS-specs-coverage.md — derived status summary (never hand-edited
directly).
If you add or modify an instruction, CSR, privilege behavior, or memory rule,
you must update the first two and re-derive the third.Living traceability documents are essential because hardware knowledge decays
quickly. A test suite may pass today but become obsolete when the next
extension is added; an implementation may be complete for one target but
incomplete for another. By maintaining both a forward map (spec chapter → RTL)
and a reverse map (RTL → test suite), CVA6 creates a closed loop. The derived
AGENTS-specs-coverage.md summary is the dashboard that tells a project manager,
a contributor, or an agent which areas are solid and which are honest gaps.
data.2-device-tree-as-the-soc-contract#2. Dev:
Linux device-tree properties are the SoC-visible contract of what the core
implements. Each property maps to a config knob and a spec anchor. The standing
rule is: any change to a device-tree-visible capability must update
AGENTS-dts-validation.md.The device tree is the boundary between hardware and operating-system software.
Unlike a register map, which describes how to operate a device, the device tree
describes what the platform is: how many cores, which extensions, how much
cache, where the memory lives, which interrupt controllers exist. When this
description is wrong, the kernel may boot but fail to use a peripheral, or it
may configure itself for a different microarchitecture. The standing rule to
update AGENTS-dts-validation.md on every device-tree-visible change is
therefore not documentation hygiene; it is a correctness gate for software
bring-up.Key mappings:
.dts property	Config knob	Spec anchor	riscv,isa	Extension bits in cva6_cfg_t	Vol I base + extension chapters	mmu-type	vm_mode_t	Sv32/Sv39/Sv48/Sv57	i-cache-size, d-cache-size	IcacheByteSize, DcacheByteSize	Zic64b, PMA, CMO	memory@<base>	Axi*Width + region rules	Address-space introduction, PMA	clint@, plic@	corev_apu/clint, corev_apu/rv_plic	Privileged interrupts/timers	
The script build-platform/scripts/fetch-linux-dts.{sh,ps1} populates the
upstream Linux DTS reference used by AGENTS-dts-validation.md.
data.core#Core:
Spec first: an instruction or CSR must have a real encoding and a spec
anchor before RTL.
Config gate: every new feature is gated in cva6_cfg_t and has a
check_cfg legality assertion.
Discovery: the ISA string (misa) must expose the feature so that
OpenSBI / Linux / toolchain can see it.
DTS: cache sizes, MMU type, and interrupt/timer nodes must match the
config.
data.controllers-corev_apu--vendor#Controller:
Spec second-order: controllers are not in the RISC-V instruction-set spec,
but they must honor the platform's memory and interrupt model (PMA, PMP, AXI
ordering, interrupt IDs).
AXI seam: the core's memory-side port is AXI. Controllers connect through
this seam; their AXI*Width must match the core config.
PHY split: a controller (digital) and its PHY (analog/hard macro) are
often separate IP. The board layer (corev-mb) records which PHY is used and
how pins map.
DTS: controller nodes (clint, plic, ethernet, etc.) are described in the
board .dts and must match the enabled controllers.
Controllers are where the RISC-V platform model meets the messy reality of
peripheral IP. An Ethernet MAC does not appear in the unprivileged ISA, but it
must obey the platform's memory ordering, interrupt routing, and clock/reset
rules. The PHY split matters because the digital controller is usually
synthesizable SystemVerilog that can be simulated, while the PHY is often an
analog hard macro or an external chip whose behavior is characterized by
datasheets and SPICE models. Keeping these layers separate in the worktree —
controller in corev_apu/, PHY in corev-mb/ — mirrors the separation between
digital and analog design teams in a real SoC program.
data.motherboard-corev-mb-and-phy#Motherboard:
Board spec source of truth: corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json declares the
SoC core config, enabled controllers, and physical interfaces/PHYs.
PHY development: a PHY is not RTL in the traditional sense; it is an
analog/mixed-signal block or a hard macro. The board layer records PHY
identity, pin mapping, power rails, and timing constraints, while the APU
layer contains the digital controller.
DTS alignment: the board's generated or hand-written .dts must match
board.json and the enabled controllers. g6lc-build mb select <id> adapts
the SoC config and vendor sync to match.
Power / placement: custom boards use SKiDL + pcbparts.dev to select parts,
plan power rails, and run ERC. See SKiDL process.
data.4-the-configts--dts--spec-triple#4. The:
The repo-root .config.ts is the human/AI-editable control surface. It must be
consistent with:
core/include/*config_pkg.sv — the SystemVerilog config structs.
corev_apu/bootrom/*.dts and corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json — the
device-tree view.
specs/riscv-spec.html — the normative ISA behavior.
A feature is fully integrated only when all three are aligned and the matching
rows in AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md / AGENTS-specs-to-tests.md /
AGENTS-dts-validation.md are updated.The triple-alignment rule is deceptively simple and devastatingly effective.
Misalignment between .config.ts and cva6_cfg_t means the RTL does not match
the build description. Misalignment between .config.ts and .dts means
OpenSBI or Linux will see a different platform than the one the RTL implements.
Misalignment between .dts and specs/riscv-spec.html means the operating
system will expect ISA behavior that the core does not provide. The agent
checklist at the end of this page forces every ISA-visible change to cross
these three boundaries explicitly, which is exactly the discipline required
for a chip that must boot real software.
data.5-for-ai-agents#5. For AI agents:
When asked to add an ISA-visible feature, an LLM agent should:
Open AGENTS.md and find the relevant agents/spec/ sub-file and
agents/guides/ entry.
Read the spec anchor in specs/riscv-spec.html.
Update or verify cva6_cfg_t in core/include/config_pkg.sv.
Implement at the sanctioned seam (CVXIF, tc_sram, AXI adapter, etc.).
Update AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md and the test map.
If the feature changes a device-tree-visible property, update
AGENTS-dts-validation.md and the relevant .dts.
Run g6lc-build test --open-source (or the relevant suite) before declaring
done.

This page describes the purpose of each top-level directory at a level high
enough to stay current as files move. For exact file lists, see the repository
itself.A repository's directory structure is its long-term API. When a new engineer or
an automated agent opens the project, the first question is not "what does this
file do?" but "what is the shape of the system?" The CVA6 worktree is designed
so that the shape itself communicates intent: directories that hold compiled
IP are separated from directories that hold configuration, tooling, and
non-compiled design exploration. Understanding this shape is prerequisite to
every other activity in the project, because every edit is evaluated by whether
it respects the seams between these directories.
data.core--the-risc-v-cpu#core/ — the RISC-V:
Source code for the CVA6 core only. It should contain no code needed to build
anything other than the core. Key subdirectories:
include/ — SystemVerilog packages and config structs (config_pkg.sv,
cv64a6_*_config_pkg.sv, etc.). The cva6_cfg_t struct is the single source
of truth for feature gating.
frontend/ — fetch, branch prediction (BTB, BHT, RAS), and instruction
queue.
cache_subsystem/ — L1 instruction/data caches, AXI adapters, and the
HPDcache integration.
cva6_mmu/ — MMU, page-table walker (PTW), shared TLB.
pmp/ — physical memory protection.
perf_counters.sv, cva6_rvfi*.sv — observability and RVFI trace.
The core is the most spec-bound layer: every ISA-visible change must update
AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md, AGENTS-specs-to-tests.md, and the derived
AGENTS-specs-coverage.md.The core's isolation is its most valuable property. In commercial practice, a
core that can be compiled, simulated, and synthesized stand-alone can be reused
across multiple SoCs, sold as soft IP, or retargeted to new processes without
dragging along board-specific wrappers. CVA6 enforces this isolation at the
file-system level: nothing in core/ references corev_apu/ or corev-mb/.
This one-way dependency is the difference between a reusable IP block and a
monolithic design that can only be used in its original context.
data.corev_apu--on-die-uncore--fpga-emulation:
The CORE-V-APU wraps the core for FPGA emulation and SoC integration. It depends
on core/ but the core does not depend on it. Key areas:
src/ — top-level APU wrapper, AXI crossbar, interrupt controllers, timers,
bootrom, and FPGA-specific glue.
axi_mem_if/ — AXI memory interface.
bootrom/ — first-stage boot code and the .dts source.
clint/, rv_plic/ — standard RISC-V interrupt/timer blocks.
fpga/ — FPGA synthesis constraints and scripts.
Vendored controllers and PHY (DDR, Ethernet, PCIe, etc.) are fetched into the
APU layer by the build-platform vendor command; they are not committed as raw
copies. See AGENTS-vendor.md and AGENTS-corev-apu.md.The APU layer is where the economics of integration become visible. Vendors
typically charge for controllers and PHYs under NDA or license, and those IP
blocks evolve on their own schedules. By fetching rather than copying, CVA6
keeps the vendored IP in a form that can be updated, scanned for known issues,
and audited for license compatibility. The APU layer's job is to hold the
digital controllers and the AXI fabric that stitches them to the core, while
leaving the analog PHY and board-specific details to the board layer.
data.corev-mb--motherboard--board-layer#corev:
The board around the die. It is non-compiled scaffolding plus a small Python
library for custom board design with SKiDL.
boards/<id>/ — each board has a board.json machine spec and a
generated/ directory (gitignored) for <id>_board_pkg.sv and board.mk.
architecture/<id>/ — non-compiled development-target documentation.
lib/ — SKiDL helper scripts and pcbparts_mcp.py (MCP client for
pcbparts.dev part selection).
Selecting a board (g6lc-build mb select <id>) adapts the SoC config, syncs
the board's vendored controllers, and generates the board package. See
AGENTS-motherboard.md.The board layer is the most concrete reminder that a CPU is not a software
artifact. A chip must live on a board, surrounded by power regulators, memory,
connectors, and PHYs. The corev-mb layer treats the board as a configuration
problem: board.json describes the machine, and the build platform generates
the artifacts needed to parameterize the APU. This decouples board
specification from RTL editing, which is essential when multiple boards share
the same core or when one board goes through multiple revisions.
data.verif--verification#verif/ — verificatio:
The verification environment. It includes:
regress/ — one script per regression suite; catalogued by the build
platform.
tests/ — test programs and testlist_*.yaml files.
sim/ — DV/UVM and riscv-dv environment.
tb/ — testbench modules.
bsp/ — board support package for test programs.
core-v-verif/ is a submodule that contains verification files shared with
other OpenHW cores.Verification is not a downstream activity in CVA6; it is a first-class
deliverable whose structure mirrors the design itself. regress/ contains the
orchestration scripts that the build platform catalogues; tests/ contains the
programs and test lists; sim/ and tb/ contain the environments that execute
them. By keeping verification at the same directory level as the core and APU,
the project signals that a feature is not complete until it is verified, not
when it is coded. The core-v-verif submodule further reflects the OpenHW
collaborative model: common verification infrastructure is shared across cores,
while core-specific tests live here.
data.vendor--third-party-ip#vendor/ — third-p:
Controllers and utility IP maintained outside the repository. It includes the
pulp-platform AXI, common_cells, and riscv-isa-manual submodules. The build
platform's vendor command can fetch additional controllers and PHY into
corev_apu/vendor/. See AGENTS-vendor.md.Vendor IP management is one of the most legally and technically sensitive
activities in SoC design. The vendor/ directory holds utility IP that is
explicitly open-source and maintained as a submodule, while the build platform's
vendor command handles additional controllers and PHYs that may arrive as
snapshots, submodules, or NDA drops. This distinction matters because it
separates "always present infrastructure" from "on-demand integration,"
preventing the repository from accumulating stale or unlicensed copies of
third-party code.
data.build-platform--automation-spine#build-p:
A Bun + TypeScript project that drives the whole flow from .config.ts. It is
parameterized, cross-platform, and contained: everything it installs or produces
goes into build-platform/workspace/.
src/cli/ — command registry (status, probe, diag, verify, timings,
vendor, mb, tech, …).
src/config/ — schema, defaults, and config loader.
src/tooling/ — tool detection, install recipes, vendor sync, motherboard
engine, pcbparts MCP client, technology engine, and timings host adapter.

collection of files into a reproducible workflow. Its containment in
build-platform/workspace/ is a deliberate isolation choice: anything the
platform installs, downloads, or produces is disposable. This means CI runners,
new laptops, and automated agents can all start from a clean state and reach
the same result. The platform's typed config surface also makes it the natural
place for an LLM to read the SoC state before deciding which command to run.See Build Platform, Probe, Diag & Verify,

follows the substructure map to the relevant AGENTS-*.md and agents/guides/
file for the task, then opens the spec sub-files and code loci listed there.
This keeps the context window small and the reasoning grounded.

This page is the practical counterpart to AGENTS-coding-philosophy.md and
AGENTS-configuration.md. It explains the patterns that keep CVA6 synthesizable,
timing-clean, and verifiable as the architecture grows.CPU architecture is a discipline of constraint. Unlike software, where an
incorrect result can be patched and re-deployed, an incorrect CPU may require a
new mask set, a board re-spin, or a product recall. The guidelines below are
therefore not stylistic preferences; they are risk-mitigation patterns derived
from the experience of taping out in-order RISC-V cores and integrating them
into real products.
data.1-correctness-before-performance#1. Corr:
Baseline CVA6 is an in-order core with precise speculation and a short critical
path. This branch may enable config-gated multi-issue, slice-OoO, full OoO
(core/ooo/), SMT (core/smt/), and related structures — still behind
CVA6Cfg so minimal targets elaborate as the classic machine. The first
question is always: does this change preserve ISA semantics? The second
question is: does it close timing? A performance improvement that lengthens
the critical path is not an improvement for silicon.For structural path feedback before STA, use sv-timing /
g6lc-build timings (FO4 estimates only).This ordering of priorities is non-negotiable for physical design. A core that
passes architectural tests but fails timing at the target frequency cannot be
shipped. In practice, this means architects and RTL engineers must collaborate
with synthesis and place-and-route engineers early, not as a hand-off at the
end. The most common source of timing surprises is a "small" microarchitectural
change that adds a multiplexer or comparator in the wrong place. CVA6's short,
pipelined structure makes it sensitive to such changes, which is why every PR
should include a timing impact note.
data.2-timing-as-a-first-class-citizen#2. Tim:
Keep combinational cones short.
Add pipeline stages for complex units rather than widening a single stage.
Avoid high fan-in / fan-out nets that create routing hotspots.
Every new unit needs an early-synthesis loop (see pd/synth/) and a timing
impact note in the PR.
data.3-modularity-through-cva6cfg#3. Modulari:
CVA6Cfg is not just a parameter bundle; it is the contract between the
config layer and the RTL. Every module that receives it can gate behavior
structurally:
if (CVA6Cfg.DCacheType == config_pkg::WT) begin : gen_wt_cache
  // ...
end else begin : gen_hpdcache
  // ...
end
Per-target packages (cv64a6_imafdc_sv39_config_pkg.sv, etc.) instantiate
cva6_cfg_t with concrete values. A new target = a new package, not a new RTL
file.Structural gating with CVA6Cfg has a subtle but important benefit: it makes
the cost of a feature visible. When a developer adds an if statement based on
a config bit, synthesis will physically remove the unused branch for targets
that do not enable the feature. This is the hardware equivalent of conditional
compilation, but it is more robust because it happens inside the same
SystemVerilog source and is checked by the type system. It also makes formal
verification easier, because the config space is explicit rather than implicit
in ifdef soup.
data.4-single-reset-single-clock-domain-by-de:
Use asynchronous-active-low reset:
always_ff @(posedge clk_i or negedge rst_ni).
Do not add a new clock or asynchronous reset without explicit CDC/reset-sync
analysis.
The only sanctioned latch is inside tc_clk_gating in the tech-cells generic.
data.5-simulation-only-code-belongs-behind-tr:
Assertions, display statements, and other non-synthesizable debug code must be
fenced with:
//pragma translate_off
// ...
//pragma translate_on
This keeps the synthesis view clean.Translate pragmas are the boundary between the model and the artifact. In
simulation, assertions and displays are invaluable for debug. In synthesis,
they are either ignored or cause errors. By fencing them explicitly, CVA6
ensures that the netlist the foundry receives is exactly the netlist the
engineer intended. This discipline is especially important when tools are
chained: a display statement that slips into synthesis can break the entire
ASIC flow at the worst possible moment.
data.6-backend-friendly-memory-and-power#6. B:
Use tc_sram for arrays; do not instantiate raw flops for large memories.
Use tc_clk_gating for clock gating.
Use tc_pwr cells for power-aware placement.
These cells are the PDK-swap seam: a foundry drop-in replaces them at the
technology-optimization pass.
The tc_* cells are the PDK-swap seam for a reason. Memory compilers produce
DRAMs, SRAMs, and register files with foundry-specific bit cells, redundancy,
and BIST wrappers. Clock gating cells have specific enable polarities and
timing arcs. Power cells implement isolation, retention, and level shifting.
By routing every one of these through a generic wrapper, CVA6 allows the generic
RTL to be technology-agnostic and the technology pass to bind foundry-specific
views without forking the source. This is how commercial IP houses maintain a
single RTL base across dozens of process nodes.
data.7-verification-parity#7. Verification pa:
A change is not done until:
A directed test exists.
The compliance regression is still green.
Formal properties or coverage are updated if applicable.
DFT hooks (test_en_i, testmode_i) are preserved.
PMU events and RVFI probes are added or updated.
data.8-ecosystem-contract#8. Ecosystem contra:
New instructions and CSRs must have:
A real encoding.
A config bit that flows to misa / the ISA string.
DTS alignment if Linux sees it.
Toolchain / OpenSBI / Linux visibility stated in the PR.
The ecosystem contract is what makes a CPU feature useful outside the RTL. A
new instruction that the core executes but the compiler does not emit is dead
code. A CSR that Linux does not know how to read is invisible. The misa
register and the ISA string are the discovery mechanism by which the boot
firmware and operating system learn what the core can do. Violating this
contract is a common source of "the core passes tests but the board won't boot"
bugs.
data.9-prefer-sanctioned-seams#9. Prefer sanc:
When in doubt, add at a seam rather than inside a pipeline stage:
Feature type	Seam	Custom compute	CVXIF coprocessor (core/cvxif_fu.sv, core/acc_dispatcher.sv)	New memory macro	tc_sram wrapper + pd/pdk/ drop-in	New cache subsystem	cva6_cfg_t cache-type enum + core/cva6.sv selection	New branch predictor	bp_type_t + core/frontend/	OoO / slice / multi-issue	CVA6Cfg gates + core/ooo/, core/cva6_slice_*.sv, issue width	SMT	core/smt/ + target packages (see architecture/multi-threading/)	L2/L3	memory-side / corev_apu — not an L1-only edit	Structural timing feedback	sv-timing/ via g6lc-build timings (host only)	New uncore controller	corev_apu/src/ AXI seam + build-platform vendor catalog
Before proposing a core RTL edit:
Config-gated in cva6_cfg_t with check_cfg assertion.
Synth-clean (always_ff/always_comb, no new latch/clock).
Timing-aware (no long combinational path, impact note attached).
Backend-friendly (tc_sram, tc_clk_gating, tc_pwr).
Verified (directed test + regression + formal/coverage as needed).
Testable (DFT hooks preserved).
Observable (RVFI/trace, PMU, debug trigger).
Ecosystem-safe (encoding/discovery, DTS alignment).
Documented (this site + relevant AGENTS-*.md updated).
This checklist is the minimum bar for a core change. It is deliberately not
exhaustive; a complex change may also require micro-architectural review,
power analysis, security review, and formal verification. But no core change
should be proposed without these items, because each one corresponds to a
question that will be asked during code review or silicon sign-off. Treating
the checklist as a prerequisite rather than a postscript is the difference
between a feature that merges cleanly and one that creates a month of follow-up
work.

This page is a concrete playbook for an LLM agent (Devin, grok-build, or
otherwise) that is asked to modify the CVA6 CPU core.A CPU core is a high-stakes target for automated editing. Unlike a web
application, where a bug can be rolled back with a deployment, a CPU bug may not
be discovered until silicon returns from the foundry. The agent workflow for
core development is therefore conservative: it requires the agent to ground
every proposed change in the spec, the config struct, and the sanctioned seam
before writing any RTL. This conservatism is not an obstacle to productivity;
it is the discipline that makes productivity possible at scale.
data.intent-resolution#Intent resolution:
The agent receives a prompt such as:
"Add a configurable branch-target buffer size to CVA6."
The first step is not to search the whole tree. The first step is to open
AGENTS.md and resolve the intent to a small set of guide files:
AGENTS.md §3 → agents/guides/AGENTS-branch-prediction.md.
AGENTS-branch-prediction.md → spec anchors and code loci.
agents/spec/riscv-spec-I-*.html or agents/spec/riscv-spec-II-*.html for
the relevant subchapter.
The first step is the most important. A common failure mode for LLM agents on
large repositories is to search the entire tree and then synthesize a plan from
fragments. This produces plausible-looking but contextually wrong edits. By
starting at AGENTS.md, the agent loads a curated, expert-written map that
tells it which spec chapters, code loci, and checklists are relevant. This is
the hardware-engineering equivalent of starting with the design document instead
of grep.
data.plan-the-change#Plan the change:
From the guides, the agent extracts:
Spec constraint: branches and jumps must behave as architecturally
defined; predictor sizing is microarchitectural.
Config seam: CVA6Cfg.BTBEntries exists; may need a new field.
Code loci: core/frontend/btb.sv, core/frontend/frontend.sv.
Verification: arch smoke tests + formal equivalence (same branch
outcomes).
Traceability: update AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md only if the ISA-visible
behavior changes; branch predictor sizing usually does not.
The plan produced at this stage is a reasoning contract. It separates
microarchitectural changes (such as BTB sizing) from ISA-visible changes (such
as new instructions). This separation matters because microarchitectural
changes need architectural verification — the same branch outcomes must occur —
while ISA-visible changes need compliance verification against the spec. The
agent that gets this distinction right will produce a focused, reviewable PR;
the agent that conflates them will produce a broad, risky change.
data.edit-sequence#Edit sequence:
Config. Add the new field to cva6_cfg_t and the relevant target
packages. Add a check_cfg assertion.
RTL. Modify btb.sv to use the new parameter; keep the generic path
byte-for-byte when the field equals the old default.
Tests. Add or update a directed test and a smoke suite.
Docs. Update the relevant AGENTS-*.md and this docs site if the user
experience changes.
The edit sequence is deliberately config-first. Many engineers, human or
automated, are tempted to open the module first because that is where the
"real" logic lives. But in a config-driven core, the struct is the contract
that the rest of the system reads. Changing the module before the struct is
like changing a function implementation before updating its signature: it may
compile in isolation, but it will not integrate. The agent must prove that the
new field is legal and visible before using it.
data.validate#Validate:
g6lc-build test --group arch --dry-run   # see what would run
g6lc-build test --group arch             # run it (requires toolchain)
The build platform preflights tool availability. If the toolchain is not
installed, the suite is skipped with a reason, not failed.Preflight is the agent's safety net. It prevents the agent from concluding that
a change is broken when the only problem is a missing tool. It also prevents
the agent from running suites that require UVM or proprietary simulators on a
laptop that only has Verilator. This graceful degradation is essential for
automated workflows that must run across heterogeneous environments.
data.common-agent-mistakes#Common agent mista:
Editing modules before config. Always extend cva6_cfg_t first.
Ignoring the critical path. A larger BTB may add area but should not
lengthen the access path.
Forgetting observability. Add or update PMU events for the changed
structure.
Skipping traceability. Even microarchitectural changes may need a note in
AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md if they affect observable timing or cache behavior.
data.when-to-escalate#When to escalate:
Escalate to a human (or a deeper design doc) when:
The change crosses clock domains or requires CDC analysis.
The change modifies the memory model or exception semantics.
The change requires a new PDK cell or foundry view.
The change is larger than a single config + module pair.
Escalation is not failure; it is risk management. The items above are exactly
the boundaries where an automated agent's reasoning can become underconstrained.
Clock-domain crossing, memory-model changes, and PDK cells all have physical
consequences that require human judgment or specialized tools. A well-designed
agent workflow knows when to stop and ask, rather than guessing and creating
silicon-debug work later.

data:
The corev_apu layer is where on-die digital controllers connect to the CVA6
core. The analog or board-side PHY is described in corev-mb/. This split is
intentional: a controller can be reused across boards, while the PHY and pin
mapping are board-specific.The controller/PHY split is one of the most important organizational decisions
in SoC design. A digital controller is a synchronous logic block that can be
simulated, linted, and synthesized with standard RTL tools. A PHY is a
mixed-signal or analog block that is characterized by timing diagrams, IBIS
models, SPICE decks, and foundry hard-macros. Treating them as a single unit
leads to two predictable failures: the digital team modifies the controller
assuming a PHY behavior that is only valid for one board, and the board team
selects a PHY that the controller cannot drive. The CVA6 directory structure
enforces this separation so that each team can work against a stable contract.
data.controller-taxonomy#Controller taxonomy:
A controller is digital RTL that speaks a standard interface (usually AXI or an
SoC-internal bus). A PHY is the mixed-signal or hard-macro block that sits at
the chip edge and drives pads, SerDes, or analog front-ends.Examples:
Function	Controller (in corev_apu / vendor)	PHY (in corev-mb / PDK)	DDR3/4	MIG / vendor DDR controller	DDR PHY on the board or hard macro in the SoC	Ethernet	ariane-ethernet / vendor MAC	RTL8211E / external PHY	PCIe	vendor root complex	PHY hard macro	UART	simple APB/APB-lite UART	FT2232HQ / level shifter
data.axi-seam#AXI seam:
The core's memory-side port is AXI. Controllers connect through this seam. The
critical parameters are:
AxiAddrWidth
AxiDataWidth
AxiIdWidth
AxiUserWidth
These must match between the core config, the crossbar, and the controller. The
mb select step generates a board package that exports AxiDataWidth and
feature enables so the APU wrapper can parameterize correctly.The AXI seam is the universal socket of the CVA6 memory system. AXI's
standardized address, data, ID, and user channels allow controllers from
different vendors and authors to coexist on the same fabric, but only if their
parameters match. Mismatched AxiDataWidth causes silent data corruption;
mismatched AxiIdWidth causes ID aliasing and ordering violations. The board
package exists precisely to export these widths as localparams so the APU
can instantiate the core and controllers with a single, consistent view.
data.adding-a-vendored-controller#Adding a ve:
Catalog. Add a VendorControllerSpec to .config.ts or
build-platform/src/config/defaults.ts with id, description, domain,
kind, mechanism (submodule / snapshot), url, path, license,
scanPaths, integrationSeam, phyNote, and architectureDoc.
Fetch. Run g6lc-build vendor sync <id>. The platform fetches or updates
the IP and runs the scan step if configured.
Integrate. Wire the controller into the APU at the declared seam,
respecting AGENTS-corev-apu.md preconditions.
Board. If the controller needs a PHY, update corev-mb/ board JSON and
the per-board AGENTS-mb-<id>.md contract.
DTS. Add or update device-tree nodes for the controller and its
interrupts.
Cataloging a controller is not merely bookkeeping. The catalog fields record
where the IP comes from, how it is fetched, what license governs it, and
which seam it integrates through. This metadata is what allows the build
platform to automate vendor sync and the legal review to confirm that the
resulting product is distributable. Skipping the catalog and copying files by
hand destroys this traceability and creates a hidden compliance debt.
data.phy-development-considerations#PHY devel:
A PHY is not authored like RTL. It is selected, placed, and constrained:
Part selection — for board PHYs, use g6lc-build mb parts (pcbparts.dev
MCP) or the corev-mb/lib/pcbparts_mcp.py client.
Pin mapping — record PHY pins and their SoC pad mappings in the board
contract.
Power rails — the board's SKiDL flow plans power domains and ERC.
Timing — PHY interfaces (RGMII, DDR, PCIe, etc.) have skew and delay
constraints captured in the board/fpga constraints.
Hard macros — for SoC-integrated PHYs, the foundry provides a hard macro
that is bound at the PDK-swap seam during the technology optimization pass.
PHY development is a different engineering culture from RTL development. It is
not about writing logic; it is about selecting parts, analyzing signal
integrity, planning power rails, and capturing skew constraints. For a board
PHY such as an RGMII Ethernet transceiver, the critical question is whether the
SoC's output delays and the PHY's input setup/hold windows overlap across
temperature and voltage corners. For an SoC-integrated PHY, the question is
whether the foundry hard macro's interface can be driven by the digital
controller at the target frequency. The CVA6 flow pushes these questions to
the board layer and the technology pass, where the right experts and tools
live.
data.dts-alignment-for-controllers#DTS alignm:
Every enabled controller must appear consistently in:
.config.ts / cva6_cfg_t.
corev_apu/bootrom/*.dts or the board's generated .dts.
corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json.
AGENTS-dts-validation.md if it is a device-tree-visible block.
See Specs, DTS & Architecture for the
full triple-alignment rule.
data.soc-readiness-gates#SoC-readiness gates:
Before a controller/PHY integration is considered done:
AXI widths and ordering aligned with core config.
PHY identity, pin mapping, and power rails documented in board contract.
Vendor IP scanned and license recorded.
DTS nodes added/updated.
Simulation / smoke test passes.
Synthesis constraints for FPGA or ASIC target present.
DFT hooks and test-mode pins propagated.
This checklist reflects the full lifecycle of a controller integration. It
begins with protocol correctness (AXI), proceeds through legal and engineering
traceability (vendor scan, board contract), and ends with manufacturing
readiness (DFT, synthesis constraints). Each unchecked item is a risk that will
surface at a different point in the program: AXI issues in simulation, PHY
issues in board bring-up, DTS issues in Linux boot, and DFT issues in
production test. Completing the list before declaring done is what makes the
integration durable.

data:
This page describes how an LLM agent should approach a task like:
"Integrate a DDR4 controller and PHY for the genesys2 board."
Integrating an uncore controller is one of the most cross-functional tasks in
the CVA6 workflow. The agent must reason about the core config (what the CPU
can do), the controller IP (what the vendor provides), the board contract (what
PHY and pins are available), and the device tree (how Linux will see it). No
single file contains the whole picture. The agent's job is to assemble the
picture from the contracts and to make the integration pass g6lc-build mb
check and g6lc-build vendor sync.
data.step-1-resolve-intent#Step 1: Resolve in:
Open AGENTS.md §3 and find the row for vendored uncore controllers/PHY. It
points to:
AGENTS-corev-apu.md — uncore preconditions.
AGENTS-vendor.md — fetch/update/scan workflow.
AGENTS-controller-readiness.md — feature playbook.
agents/guides/AGENTS-technology-optimization.md — if the integration
requires a foundry hard macro.
Intent resolution for corev_apu is a multi-document lookup because the
relevant knowledge is distributed. AGENTS-corev-apu.md gives the uncore
preconditions; AGENTS-vendor.md explains how to fetch and scan IP;
AGENTS-controller-readiness.md gives the feature-specific playbook; and
AGENTS-technology.md is needed if the integration touches a foundry hard
macro. Reading them in sequence builds a complete plan before any file is
modified.
data.step-2-read-the-board-contract#Step 2: R:
The target board is genesys2. Open:
corev-mb/boards/genesys2/board.json — the machine spec.
AGENTS-mb-genesys2.md — per-board contract.
corev-mb/architecture/genesys2/README.md — development target notes.
These tell the agent which controllers are already enabled, which PHYs the
board uses, and what remains to be integrated.The board contract is the source of truth for the physical environment. It
tells the agent which controllers are already enabled, which PHYs the board
uses, and whether the board is a reference board or a custom SKiDL board. This
context is essential because the same controller may be used differently on
different boards. For example, an Ethernet MAC may be enabled on one board and
disabled on another, depending on whether the PHY is present and connected.
data.step-3-catalog-and-fetch-the-controller#:
The agent checks .config.ts for vendor.controllers and runs:
g6lc-build vendor list
g6lc-build vendor status <id>
g6lc-build vendor sync <id> --dry-run
g6lc-build vendor sync <id>
The --dry-run pass lets the agent confirm what will be fetched before
mutating the workspace.The dry-run discipline is especially important for vendor IP, because fetching
can modify the workspace and introduce legal obligations. By running vendor
status and vendor sync --dry-run first, the agent confirms the source, the
version, and the scan results before committing to the fetch. This is the same
discipline used in package managers such as npm or cargo, where the lock
file is inspected before dependencies are downloaded.
data.step-4-integrate-at-the-apu-seam#Step 4::
Using the integrationSeam pointer from the catalog, the agent opens the APU
top-level and wires the controller:
Match Axi*Width to the core config.
Connect clock/reset/CDC correctly.
Propagate test_en_i / testmode_i for DFT.
Keep PHY-vs-controller separation: the controller lives in corev_apu/; the
PHY details live in corev-mb/.
Integration at the APU seam is where the agent's understanding of the AXI
protocol, clock domains, and DFT is tested. The controller must be wired to a
fabric whose widths and ordering semantics match the core. The clock and reset
must be clean. And the test_en_i / testmode_i pins must be propagated so
that scan and ATPG tools can control the new logic in manufacturing test. These
are not optional niceties; they are what make the chip manufacturable.
data.step-5-board-package-and-dts#Step 5: Boa:
Run the board configure step:
g6lc-build mb select genesys2 --dry-run
g6lc-build mb select genesys2
This generates genesys2_board_pkg.sv and board.mk and updates the overlay
config. The agent then updates the .dts to match the new controller and its
interrupts, and updates AGENTS-dts-validation.md if needed.
data.step-6-verify#Step 6: Verify:
g6lc-build mb check genesys2
g6lc-build test --open-source   # if the toolchain is provisioned
The mb check command exits 3 on incompatibility, so the agent knows
immediately if the board/package handshake failed.The verification sequence closes the loop. mb check confirms that the board
and the SoC config agree; mb select generates the board package; and test
--open-source runs the architectural tests that confirm the core still behaves
correctly with the new controller. If any step fails, the agent knows exactly
where the integration broke. This is the benefit of a platform-driven workflow:
failures are localized and diagnostic, not mysterious regressions discovered
weeks later.
data.common-agent-mistakes#Common agent mista:
Mixing PHY into APU RTL. PHYs are board or PDK concerns, not corev_apu/src/.
Hard-coding widths. Widths come from cva6_cfg_t / board package.
Skipping vendor scan. Always run the scan step before integrating vendored
IP.
Forgetting the overlay. mb select writes build-platform/.config.local.ts;
the agent must not hand-edit it.

corev_apu/ is the on-die uncore and FPGA emulation platform around the
CVA6 core. It depends on core/ but the core does not depend on it. This
separation lets the core be reused in different SoCs while the APU supplies the
peripherals, memory interfaces, and board-specific glue for the reference FPGA
targets.The uncore layer is the integration boundary of an SoC. It does not implement
the instruction set, but it determines whether the core can boot Linux, access
memory, and communicate with the outside world. In CVA6, this layer is
intentionally thin: it wraps the core, provides the AXI fabric, and connects
standard RISC-V blocks and vendored controllers. The philosophy is to keep the
APU as a digital glue layer and to push analog, board, and process-specific
concerns outward to corev-mb/ and pd/pdk/.
data.what-it-contains#What it contains:
Top-level wrappers — corev_apu/src/ariane.sv and related files
instantiate the core and wire it to the AXI fabric.
AXI fabric and memory interfaces — axi_mem_if/, crossbar, adapters.
L2 / L3 / server prefetch — config-gated memory-side hierarchy under
l2_cache/, l3_cache/ — see L2 / L3 Cache.
Multi-core cluster — g6lc_cluster.sv + coherence/ — see
Multi-Core Cluster.
Bootrom — first-stage boot code and the reference .dts (incl. SMT / server
math DTS variants).
Standard RISC-V blocks — clint/, rv_plic/ for timers and interrupts
(sized for multi-hart / multi-core packages).
FPGA support — constraints and scripts under fpga/.
Ara attach — optional RVV SoC glue (g6lc_ara_attach.sv); see
Vector (RVV) & Ara.
data.design-contract#Design contract:
AGENTS-corev-apu.md is the standing governance for this layer. Before any
controller or wrapper enters an flist, it must satisfy the preconditions there:
AXI seam compatibility (address, data, ID, user widths).
Clock/reset/CDC hygiene.
PHY-vs-controller separation (the digital controller lives here; the analog
PHY is described in corev-mb/).
DFT hooks preserved.
DTS alignment with the board.
The design contract is a pre-flight checklist, not a suggestion. AXI width
mismatches are one of the most common integration bugs in SoC design, because
they may simulate correctly in simple testbenches but fail under realistic
traffic. Clock/reset/CDC hygiene is equally critical: an uncore controller that
receives an asynchronously generated clock without proper synchronization can
cause metastability in the core. The contract ensures that these issues are
addressed before a controller enters the flist, not discovered during
bring-up.
data.vendored-controllers#Vendored controller:
Most non-trivial controllers (DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, storage) are not
authored in corev_apu/; they are fetched by the build-platform vendor
command from third-party repositories or vendor snapshots and scanned before
integration. The catalog lives in .config.ts (vendor.controllers) and
build-platform/src/config/defaults.ts.Vendored controllers are the reality of modern SoC design. A contemporary SoC
may contain dozens of controllers for memory, networking, storage, display, and
security. Authoring all of them from scratch is neither feasible nor desirable;
the industry relies on a combination of in-house controllers, open-source
controllers, and licensed IP. The build platform's vendor command treats these
as dependencies rather than source: it fetches them, scans them, records their
licenses, and makes them available to the APU. This dependency model is what
allows CVA6 to integrate state-of-the-art peripherals without bloating the core
repository.
data.relationship-to-the-board#Relationship t:
A board (corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json) declares which APU controllers it
needs. When you run g6lc-build mb select <id>, the platform:
Checks compatibility between the board's required core config and the current
.config.ts.
Syncs the vendored controllers the board requires.
Generates a <id>_board_pkg.sv and board.mk under
corev-mb/boards/<id>/generated/.
The APU itself is not edited by board selection; it is configured by the
resulting board package.
data.agent-workflow#Agent workflow:
See Agent Workflow for corev_apu and
Controllers & PHY.The agent workflow for corev_apu is integration-heavy. The agent must read
multiple contracts (controller, board, technology) before making a change,
because a controller that is correct in isolation may be incompatible with the
chosen board or core config. This multi-contract reading is the core skill of
SoC integration: the ability to hold the core, the controller, the board, and
the DTS in alignment at the same time.

The corev-mb board layer sits around the die and is the PCB counterpart
to the SoC integration layer. Its job is to describe the physical board, the
SoC pins, the PHYs, the power rails, and the constraints that allow the die to
boot on that board.The board layer is the bridge between the digital SoC and the physical world.
Whereas the core and APU are described in SystemVerilog and simulated in
cycles, the board is described in schematics, constraints, and placement. The
corev-mb layer captures the board-specific information that the APU needs to
know — pin mappings, PHY identities, controller enables — and leaves the rest
to the board house's layout tools. This separation of concerns is what allows
the same RTL to be reused across many physical products.
data.board--machine-spec#Board = machine spec:
A board is fully described by corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json. It is the
source of truth for:
Which CVA6 core config the board expects.
Which APU controllers are enabled.
Which interfaces exist (UART, Ethernet, SD, etc.).
Which PHYs are present and how they connect to SoC pins.
Whether SKiDL is used (omitted, reference, or custom).
This JSON is read by build-platform/src/tooling/motherboard.ts.Treating a JSON file as the source of truth is a form of configuration-driven
design. It means that the board is not buried inside a Makefile or a
generated SystemVerilog file; it is an artifact that humans can read, diff, and
review. When the board changes, the JSON changes first, and the build platform
propagates that change to the generated board package, the vendor sync list,
and the overlay config. This reversibility is important: an engineer can look
at board.json and know exactly what the board is supposed to be.
data.from-boardjson-to-board-package#From boa:
When g6lc-build mb select <id> runs, the platform:
Loads and validates board.json.
Compares board.core against the current .config.ts soc.coreConfig.
For each enabled controller, runs g6lc-build vendor sync <controllerId>.
Generates corev-mb/boards/<id>/generated/<id>_board_pkg.sv with localparams
such as:
CoreConfig
Xlen
AxiDataWidth
SocketEn
MbCtrl_<id>_En
MbIf_<ID>_En, MbIf_<ID>_Count, MbIf_<ID>_Phy
Generates corev-mb/boards/<id>/generated/board.mk.
Writes the overlay build-platform/.config.local.ts to pin soc.* and
motherboard.activeBoard.
The APU wrapper imports <id>_board_pkg.sv and parameterizes itself from these
localparams. The core and APU source files are never edited by this step.This generation model is the key to board reuse. The core and APU source files
remain generic; the board package supplies the target-specific parameters.
Because the package is generated from a typed JSON spec, the parameters are
consistent with the rest of the build configuration. There is no risk that a
manual edit to a localparam will drift out of sync with .config.ts or
board.json.
data.phy-development-on-the-board#PHY develop:
A PHY is a physical-layer device. It may be:
On-board — e.g. Realtek RTL8211E for RGMII Ethernet, FT2232HQ for USB-UART.
In-package — a hardened PHY macro supplied by the foundry.
Off-chip — e.g. a DDR DIMM's SPD/termination logic.
The board layer records:
PHY identity and datasheet references.
SoC pin ↔ PHY pin mapping.
Power rails and decoupling.
Timing and skew constraints.
Reset/clock distribution.
A PHY is not software-addressable in the way a CSR is; it is a physical device
with analog characteristics. The board layer records enough information about
the PHY and its connections for the APU to instantiate the correct digital
controller and for the board house to design the surrounding circuitry. The
actual signal-integrity work — trace length matching, impedance control,
crosstalk analysis — happens in the board layout tool, but the constraints
that drive it come from the contract captured here.For custom boards, the SKiDL flow automates part selection, net creation, and
ERC. See SKiDL Process.
data.compatibility-check#Compatibility check:
g6lc-build mb check <id>
Exits 0 if the board is compatible with the current SoC config, 3 if not.
Incompatibility usually means the core config (XLEN, extensions, cache type) in
.config.ts does not match the board's core field.The compatibility check is the gate that prevents impossible boards from being
built. A board cannot make the core have more extensions than the configured
core supports; it cannot enable a 64-bit bus on a 32-bit core; and it cannot use
a cache type that the core does not implement. By enforcing these invariants
before generation, the platform prevents subtle mismatches that would only
appear during Linux boot or FPGA bring-up.
data.soc-readiness-gates-for-board-work#SoC-r:
board.json is valid and checked into corev-mb/boards/<id>/.
AGENTS-mb-<id>.md per-board contract exists and cross-references the
board JSON and architecture doc.
PHY pin mappings and power rails are documented.
mb select <id> generates the board package cleanly.
DTS matches the generated board package.
Simulation or CI smoke for the board target passes.
These gates are the board-layer equivalent of the SoC-readiness checklist. They
cover the specification (board.json), the contract (AGENTS-mb-<id>.md), the
physical mapping (PHY, power rails), the generation flow (mb select), the
software contract (DTS), and the functional validation (smoke tests). A board
that passes all these gates is ready to move from design into layout,
prototype, and eventually production.

This page walks through an LLM agent task like:
"Port CVA6 to a new milkv-jupiter board."
Porting CVA6 to a new board is not a coding task in the traditional sense; it
is a specification and integration task. The agent must discover what the
board's core, controllers, PHYs, and connectors are, then express that
discovery in board.json and the per-board contract. The goal is not to write
new RTL but to configure the existing RTL to run correctly on the new physical
platform. This makes board porting a natural fit for an agent that can read and
synthesize multiple contracts.
data.step-1-load-the-governance#Step 1: Load:
The agent opens AGENTS.md and resolves the motherboard intent:
AGENTS-motherboard.md — board-layer governance.
AGENTS-mb-skidl.md — SKiDL design philosophy.
AGENTS-mb-<id>.md for existing similar boards (e.g. AGENTS-mb-genesys2.md).
corev-mb/architecture/<id>/README.md if the target is already documented.
Governance loading is especially important for board work because the board
layer is the most physically constrained layer. AGENTS-motherboard.md gives
the rules; AGENTS-mb-skidl.md gives the design philosophy; and an existing
per-board contract such as AGENTS-mb-genesys2.md gives a concrete example of
what a finished board port looks like. Reading the architecture README tells the
agent whether the target is already understood or whether it is an analysis-only
exploration.
data.step-2-decide-board-class#Step 2: Decide:
The board class determines the flow:
Reference / third-party: skidl: "omitted". The agent writes the board
JSON, contract, and architecture doc; no SKiDL design.
Custom: skidl: "custom". The agent runs the SKiDL loop.
Reference starting point: skidl: "reference". Reuse a reference
schematic but parameterize it.
data.step-3-author-boardjson#Step 3: Author b:
The agent creates corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json with:
core matching the target CVA6 config.
apu.controllers listing only the controllers the board actually has.
interfaces and phys describing external PHYs and connectors.
skidl mode.
Authoring board.json is the central act of board porting. It requires the
agent to reconcile four inputs: the CVA6 core config that the board can support,
the controllers that are physically present, the PHYs and connectors that are
wired to the SoC, and the SKiDL mode that determines how the schematic is
produced. A mistake at this stage propagates into the generated board package,
the vendor sync list, and the DTS. The agent must therefore validate the JSON
against the build platform before proceeding.
data.step-4-compatibility-and-select#Step 4::
g6lc-build mb check <id>
g6lc-build mb select <id> --dry-run
g6lc-build mb select <id>
The agent uses --dry-run first to see the overlay and generated artifacts
without writing them. mb check exits 3 on incompatibility, so the agent knows
immediately if the SoC config must change.The dry-run and check sequence is the board porting safety net. mb check
validates the JSON against the current SoC config and exits with a non-zero
code if they are incompatible. mb select --dry-run shows the generated
artifacts and overlay without mutating the workspace. Only after both pass does
the agent run mb select for real. This sequence prevents a malformed board
spec from corrupting the working configuration.
data.step-5-skidl-design-custom-boards-only#S:
g6lc-build mb create <id>      # scaffold design.py
g6lc-build mb design <id>      # offline, cache-first
g6lc-build mb design <id> --online --fix
g6lc-build mb expand <id>
g6lc-build mb test <id>
The agent iterates on erc.py reports. It may call the pcbparts MCP tools
(either through g6lc-build mb parts or directly via corev-mb/lib/) to find
parts and confirm pinouts.The SKiDL design loop is the equivalent of writing and compiling the
schematic. The agent starts with a scaffolded design.py, runs the design
command, reads the ERC report, fixes errors, and re-runs. The --online flag
allows the agent to query pcbparts.dev for real-time stock and pinout data;
the default offline mode uses cached or stub data for reproducibility. This
iterative loop continues until the netlist is clean and the BOM is complete.
data.step-6-documentation-and-contract#Step 6:
The agent writes or updates:
AGENTS-mb-<id>.md — the per-board contract.
corev-mb/architecture/<id>/README.md — non-compiled development notes.
AGENTS-dts-validation.md — if the board exposes new device-tree nodes.
This docs site (docs/website/pages/corev-mb/) if a new board class needs
explanation.
Documentation is not an afterthought in board porting; it is the contract that
future maintainers and automated agents will read. The per-board
AGENTS-mb-<id>.md explains the design decisions and known limitations. The
architecture/<id>/README.md captures non-compiled development notes. And the
DTS validation file records any device-tree-visible changes. Without these
documents, the board port exists only in generated files and will be lost when
they are regenerated.
data.step-7-validate-end-to-end#Step 7: Valid:
g6lc-build mb check <id>
g6lc-build mb test <id>
g6lc-build test --open-source   # once the toolchain is provisioned
data.common-agent-mistakes#Common agent mista:
Editing core/ or corev_apu/src/ to fit a board. Board selection
adapts config; it does not edit the source hierarchy.
Forgetting the overlay. build-platform/.config.local.ts is
gitignored and generated; the agent must not commit it.
Mismatching core config. The board's core field and .config.ts
soc.coreConfig must agree.
Skipping ERC. The SKiDL loop is not cosmetic; it catches power and pin
mapping errors before layout.
These mistakes are common because they violate the board-layer boundary. The
board layer is not allowed to edit the source hierarchy, and it is not allowed
to leave the overlay or ERC unvalidated. An agent that follows the prescribed
workflow — governance → JSON → check → select → SKiDL → docs → validate — will
avoid all of them. The workflow is designed to catch each mistake at the step
where it is cheapest to fix.

data:
corev-mb/ is the motherboard / board layer around the CVA6 die. It is the
board counterpart to corev_apu (the die/uncore). It describes the physical
board, the SoC-to-PHY pin mappings, the power rails, and the generated board
package that configures the APU.In SoC design, the die is only half the product. The board determines whether
the die can be powered, clocked, cooled, connected to memory, and exposed to
peripherals. The corev-mb layer treats the board as a first-class design
object, not an afterthought. By describing the board in a machine-readable JSON
file and generating the board package automatically, CVA6 ensures that the same
core can be retargeted to many physical platforms without forking the RTL.
data.what-it-contains#What it contains:
boards/<id>/board.json — machine spec, source of truth for each board.
boards/<id>/generated/ — gitignored <id>_board_pkg.sv and board.mk
produced by g6lc-build mb select <id>.
architecture/<id>/README.md — non-compiled development-target documentation.
lib/ — SKiDL helper scripts and pcbparts_mcp.py for part selection.
data.design-contract#Design contract:
AGENTS-motherboard.md is the standing governance for this layer. The board
layer is subordinate to AGENTS.md §0 and never edits core/ or
corev_apu/src/ directly. Instead, it adapts the SoC config through the
generated board package and the build-platform/.config.local.ts overlay.The subordination of the board layer to AGENTS.md §0 is a critical
architectural boundary. The board layer is not allowed to change the core or the
APU source code; it can only adapt their configuration. This rule prevents the
common anti-pattern in which every new board spawns a separate fork of the RTL.
Instead, the board layer produces a generated package and an overlay config that
parameterize the existing source. This is how a single core/APU codebase can
support a family of boards.
data.board-json#Board JSON:
Each board.json declares:
core — the target CVA6 config (e.g. cv64a6_imafdc_sv39).
apu.controllers — controllers to enable and their parameters.
interfaces — board-level interfaces (UART, Ethernet, SD, GPIO, JTAG, etc.).
phys — PHY identifiers and pin mappings.
skidl — omitted, reference, or custom depending on whether SKiDL is
used for PCB design.
board.json is more than a description; it is an executable specification. The
build platform reads it, validates it, and derives the board package from it. If
the JSON is inconsistent — for example, if it enables an Ethernet controller but
fails to list the PHY — the platform will report the mismatch rather than
silently generate an invalid package. This makes the board spec the single
place where the physical intent of the product is recorded.
data.reference-board-genesys2#Reference board:
corev-mb/boards/genesys2/ is the reference. It targets:
CVA6 config cv64a6_imafdc_sv39
DDR3 MIG
RGMII Ethernet (ariane-ethernet, disabled by default)
UART via FT2232HQ
SD quad-spi
GPIO and JTAG
The board contract AGENTS-mb-genesys2.md and the architecture notes
corev-mb/architecture/genesys2/README.md document the handshakes.
data.selecting-a-board#Selecting a board:
g6lc-build mb list
g6lc-build mb check genesys2
g6lc-build mb select genesys2 --dry-run
g6lc-build mb select genesys2
The select step:
Checks compatibility between the board's core and the current SoC config.
Writes the gitignored overlay build-platform/.config.local.ts.
Syncs the board's required vendor controllers.
Generates genesys2_board_pkg.sv and board.mk under
corev-mb/boards/genesys2/generated/.
The select step is the board equivalent of a compiler invocation: it takes a
high-level specification (board.json) and produces low-level artifacts that
the APU can consume. The overlay (build-platform/.config.local.ts) pins the
SoC and motherboard configuration for the current working directory, while the
generated board package exports parameters as SystemVerilog localparams. This
two-level parameterization keeps the build context local and the generated files
disposable.
data.custom-board-design#Custom board design:
For custom boards, the agent or engineer runs:
g6lc-build mb create <id>
g6lc-build mb design <id> [--online]
g6lc-build mb expand <id>
g6lc-build mb test <id>
These use corev-mb/lib/ Python scripts and SKiDL to plan parts, power rails,
pin mappings, and ERC. See SKiDL Process and
Agent Workflow.The custom board flow moves the design problem from manual schematic capture to
programmatic board generation. This is powerful because it allows the board to
be parameterized by the same config that drives the core and APU. A change to
the SoC pinout or the selected PHY can propagate through the SKiDL netlist,
ERC, BOM, and placement hints without manual redraw. This is the same
parameterization philosophy applied to the PCB domain.

There are two one-line entry points: the build platform (build.sh / build.ps1)
and the documentation builder (docs.sh / docs.ps1). Both bootstrap Bun if it
is missing, then delegate to the TypeScript CLI or the Next.js site. This design
choice reflects a core tenet of the LibreCore build platform: the host should not
need to be pre-configured before it can be used. In industrial settings,
engineering environments are often locked down, version-controlled, or shared
across teams. A setup process that requires manual installation of five
different package managers and toolchain versions is a reproducibility
failure waiting to happen. By wrapping the bootstrap in a single shell
function, LibreCore ensures that a clean checkout plus an internet connection is
sufficient to reach a working state. The scripts intentionally install Bun into
a user-local directory rather than a system path, mirroring best practices from
language-version managers and containerized build environments.
data.1-bootstrap-the-build-platform#1. Bootst:
# Linux / macOS / WSL / Git-Bash
source ./setenv.sh
g6lc-build status          # permanent alias: g6lc-build
# Windows PowerShell
. .\setenv.ps1
g6lc-build status
setenv.sh / setenv.ps1 put g6lc-build (and the permanent alias
g6lc-build) on your path and print the current SoC status. If Bun is not
installed, the scripts download it into ~/.bun and add it to PATH for the
current shell. This temporary PATH injection is deliberate: it means the
bootstrap is non-destructive. The rest of the environment is unchanged, and a
new shell can simply source setenv.sh again if needed. For
continuous-integration runners, the same scripts can be sourced inside a job
without requiring elevated privileges or global state mutation, which keeps the
pipeline hermetic and auditable.
data.one-off-commands-without-shell-setup#One:
./build.sh doctor
./build.sh setup --install
./build.sh test --open-source
.\build.ps1 doctor
.\build.ps1 setup --install
.\build.ps1 test --open-source
data.2-build-this-documentation-site#2. Build:
The docs site lives in docs/website and is a standard Next.js + Nextra project.
Keeping the documentation builder in the same repository as the hardware source
is a deliberate convergence of concerns. In industry, documentation drift is a
well-known failure mode: engineers update RTL, the manual lags, and new
contributors reconstruct the intended flow from stale wikis and tribal
knowledge. By making the docs a first-class build artifact that can be served
locally and exported as static HTML, CVA6 treats documentation with the same
rigor as verification. The documentation build is reproducible, versioned, and
subject to the same config-driven conventions as the SoC itself.
./docs.sh dev      # start a local dev server on http://localhost:3000
./docs.sh build    # static export to docs/website/dist
.\docs.ps1 dev
.\docs.ps1 build
Both scripts:
Check for bun and install it if missing (same bootstrap as build.sh / build.ps1).
Run bun install inside docs/website if node_modules is absent.
Run next dev or next build and exit with the same status code.
The exit-code passthrough is more important than it appears. A wrapper that
swallows the underlying status makes CI/CD integration fragile, because the
pipeline cannot distinguish success from failure. Both docs.sh and
docs.ps1 exit with the same code as the bun run invocation, so they compose
cleanly into makefiles, GitHub Actions, and local shell scripts.
data.3-first-checks#3. First checks:
After the build platform is bootstrapped:
g6lc-build probe         # deep host capability boxes (installs nothing)
g6lc-build doctor        # quick PATH readiness
g6lc-build config        # print the resolved SoC configuration
g6lc-build test --list   # list all available test suites
g6lc-build timings status  # locate sv-timing package (optional structural FO4)
probe / doctor answer can this machine run the flow? config answers
what will the flow do? and test --list answers what could be validated?
Together they give a complete readiness picture before any expensive
compilation or simulation begins.When tools are missing:
g6lc-build probe install
g6lc-build tools install sim    # or dual-hart / all / spike
g6lc-build diag run host core
g6lc-build verify --lint
See Probe, Diag & Verify and
Timings.
data.4-mental-model#4. Mental model:
LibreCore is developed from the outside in:
Config first — edit .config.ts at the repo root; it is the single
control surface.
Build platform — g6lc-build (alias g6lc-build) translates config into
toolchain setup, simulation, board adaptation, vendor sync, and technology
checks.
Layered directories — core/ is the CPU, corev_apu/ is the on-die
uncore/FPGA platform, corev-mb/ is the board, vendor/ is third-party IP,
build-platform/ is the automation spine, and sv-timing/ is an optional
independent structural-timing package.
Agent guides — AGENTS.md and its siblings answer "where in the spec and
code does this feature live?" for both humans and LLM agents.
This four-step model inverts the traditional "edit the RTL first" workflow.
Instead of opening a SystemVerilog file and hoping the surrounding environment
will adapt, the LibreCore workflow begins with the control surface and lets the
platform propagate the change through the correct seam. This outside-in
approach is what makes the project legible to automation: an LLM can read the
config, discover the relevant agent guide, and invoke the exact command needed
to verify its change without guessing at directory layout or script names.
