This page is the central playbook for an LLM agent working in the CVA6
repository. It explains the knowledge graph — the AGENTS-*.md files — and
how to traverse it from intent to verified change.An LLM agent working on a CPU core cannot read every file. Even if it could,
the raw file tree does not tell the agent what is important or how to reason
about a change. The CVA6 knowledge graph is a curated map that turns a human
intent into a sequence of documents, code loci, and commands. It is the
central nervous system of the agent workflow.
data.the-cva6-knowledge-graph#The CVA6 knowle:
The repository is not a flat directory tree; it is a graph of intents:
Intent (e.g. "add L2 cache")
    ↓
AGENTS.md §3 navigation table
    ↓
agents/guides/AGENTS-<domain>.md
    ↓
agents/spec/riscv-spec-*.html
    ↓
code loci (file.sv:start-end)
    ↓
config seam (cva6_cfg_t / .config.ts / board.json)
    ↓
build-platform command (g6lc-build ...)
    ↓
verification + traceability update
The graph has a regular shape that mirrors the engineering process. Each level
carries a different kind of truth: intent is the requirement; AGENTS.md is
the index; the domain guide is the design contract; the spec summary is the
normative reference; the code loci are the implementation; the config seam is
the integration boundary; the build command is the execution harness; and the
traceability update closes the loop. An agent that traverses this graph in
order will rarely get lost.
data.how-to-read-an-agents--file#How to read:
Every agent guide has the same anatomy:
What it is for. One sentence of intent.
Spec anchors. specs/riscv-spec.html#anchor references.
Code loci. path/to/file.sv:start-end references.
Sanctioned seam. Where to make the change.
Checklist. The SoC-readiness items that must be true before declaring done.
When an agent opens an AGENTS-*.md file, it should read it as a planning
contract, not as prose. The contract tells the agent what to open next.Reading an AGENTS-*.md file as a contract rather than prose is a discipline.
The spec anchors tell the agent which normative text governs the change. The
code loci tell the agent where to look in the RTL. The sanctioned seam tells
the agent where the change should be inserted. And the checklist tells the
agent when the change is truly complete. Skipping any of these sections is
like signing a contract without reading the clauses.
data.example-1-add-a-new-risc-v-csr#Example 1:
AGENTS.md §3 → no exact row, but AGENTS-soc-readiness.md is the
cross-cutting guide for ISA-visible changes.
AGENTS-soc-readiness.md → extend cva6_cfg_t, add encoding, update
misa/ISA string, add tests, update traceability.
agents/spec/INDEX.md → find the CSR subchapter in Volume II.
Read agents/spec/riscv-spec-II-*.html for the exact CSR semantics.
Open core/csr_regfile.sv and core/include/config_pkg.sv.
Implement, run g6lc-build test --open-source, update
AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md and AGENTS-dts-validation.md if the CSR is
visible to Linux.
data.example-2-add-an-ethernet-controller-for:
AGENTS.md §3 → AGENTS-controller-readiness.md +
AGENTS-corev-apu.md + AGENTS-vendor.md.
Read AGENTS-mb-genesys2.md and corev-mb/boards/genesys2/board.json.
Add the controller to vendor.controllers in .config.ts or defaults.
g6lc-build vendor sync <id>.
Wire the controller into corev_apu/src/ at the AXI seam.
g6lc-build mb select genesys2 to regenerate the board package.
Update .dts, AGENTS-dts-validation.md, and per-board contract.
data.example-3-run-a-foundry-technology-optim:
AGENTS.md §3 → AGENTS-technology.md +
agents/guides/AGENTS-technology-optimization.md.
Confirm technology.optimizationPass and pdkMode in .config.ts.
Author or locate *.tech-spec.md.
g6lc-build tech status → g6lc-build tech plan → g6lc-build tech check.
Add guard-macro-protected wrappers at the PDK-swap seam.
Verify equivalence, DFT, timing, power, area.
These examples are not exhaustive, but they illustrate a pattern. In each case,
the agent starts with AGENTS.md, narrows to a domain guide, reads the spec
and the board or config contract, makes a targeted change, and validates
through g6lc-build. The pattern holds whether the task is an ISA-visible
change, an uncore integration, or a technology optimization. Mastering this
pattern is what makes an agent effective on CVA6.
data.the-build-platform-as-the-agent-executor:
The agent does not run make directly. It runs g6lc-build <command>:
g6lc-build probe / doctor — host readiness (prefer probe for depth).
g6lc-build tools install … / setup --install — provision tools.
g6lc-build diag run … — compartmentalized lint/diagnostic surfaces.
g6lc-build verify --lint (etc.) — AGENTS.md §0.2 per-change gate.
g6lc-build test --<filter> — regression suites.
g6lc-build timings analyze|correct — structural FO4 via sv-timing.
g6lc-build vendor sync <id> — fetch IP.
g6lc-build mb select <id> — configure board.
g6lc-build tech check — technology readiness gates.
Each command returns an exit code and (with --json) structured output. The
agent can parse the output to decide the next step.The build platform is the agent's hands. It provisions tools, fetches IP,
configures boards, runs tests, and checks technology readiness. By delegating
to g6lc-build rather than running ad hoc commands, the agent benefits from
the platform's preflight checks, error handling, and deterministic exit codes.
The --json output makes this delegation programmatic, so an agent can read
the result and branch accordingly.
data.dry-run-discipline#Dry-run discipline:
Before any mutating command, the agent should run the --dry-run variant when
available:
g6lc-build vendor sync <id> --dry-run
g6lc-build mb select <id> --dry-run
g6lc-build tech plan
This shows what will change without writing files, so the agent can validate
its plan before execution.Dry-run is the agent's rehearsal. It is especially important for commands that
mutate the workspace, such as vendor sync, mb select, or tech init. A
dry-run shows what files will be fetched, what overlays will be written, and
what gates will be checked. It lets the agent validate that its plan is
consistent with the config before making irreversible changes. This discipline
prevents the common agent failure of "I ran a command and now the workspace is
in an unexpected state."
data.traceability-updates#Traceability update:
For ISA-visible changes, the agent must update the living traceability files:
AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md
AGENTS-specs-to-tests.md
AGENTS-specs-coverage.md (re-derived)
AGENTS-dts-validation.md (if Linux-visible)
For test suite changes, update AGENTS-specs-to-tests.md and re-derive
AGENTS-specs-coverage.md.Traceability is the agent's proof of correctness. For an ISA-visible change,
the forward map (AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md) shows where the spec requirement
was implemented, and the reverse map (AGENTS-specs-to-tests.md) shows how it
was verified. The derived coverage summary is the dashboard that tells the
project whether the change is complete. Without these updates, a change is
merely code; with them, it is an auditable engineering artifact.
data.when-to-stop-and-ask-a-human#When to sto:
An agent should escalate when:
The change touches clock domains, reset strategy, or CDC.
The change modifies the memory model or exception semantics.
The change requires a new PDK cell or foundry hard macro.
The change is larger than one config + one seam pair.
The change has unclear legal/licensing implications (vendor IP, NDA content).
Escalation criteria are the boundaries of safe automation. Each item in the
list is a domain where human judgment is currently more reliable than an LLM:
clock and reset design, memory-model semantics, foundry-specific cell
integration, large cross-cutting changes, and legal/licensing questions. An
agent that escalates early avoids creating expensive problems and preserves the
trust of the human reviewers.
data.tooling-for-agents#Tooling for agents:
File discovery: src/workspace/discovery.ts with glob patterns.
Config loading: src/config/load.ts.
Process execution: src/platform/exec.ts.
Child environment: childEnv(ctx) in src/context.ts.
These helpers keep the agent's interaction with the host deterministic and
cross-platform.The agent tooling is intentionally thin. It does not try to implement the
entire workflow in TypeScript; it provides deterministic helpers for the
operations that every command needs: finding files, loading config, running
processes, and setting up the child environment. By keeping these helpers
cross-platform, the platform ensures that an agent written for one operating
system will behave the same on another.

This site is a living, file-based guide to GSys LibreCore (shorthand
LibreCore, code prefix G6LC) — a source-available RISC-V project derived
from OpenHW Group CVA6. It is built with
Next.js and Nextra so that new
sections appear automatically as Markdown files are added under
docs/website/pages.The modern semiconductor industry is undergoing a structural shift: the
boundaries between processor design, system integration, board design, and
manufacturing are collapsing into a single continuous workflow. LibreCore sits
at the center of this shift. Unlike a research prototype that exists only as a
simulation model, the CVA6 lineage it builds on is an industrial-grade RISC-V
core that has been taped out, booted into Linux, and integrated into real SoCs.
The documentation you are reading is therefore not merely a user manual; it is
a field guide for navigating the full lifecycle of an open-source silicon
project, from the first micro-architectural idea to the final foundry sign-off.
This site treats the repository as a knowledge graph in which every
directory, config file, and agent guide has a precise role, and it explains how
those roles connect to industry practices such as design reuse, silicon
sign-off, device-tree contracts, and automated regression.
data.what-librecore-is-today#What LibreCore i:
LibreCore is a 6-stage RISC-V CPU (classically single-issue in-order; this tree
adds config-gated multi-issue, slice/full OoO, SMT, L2, and related
extensions). It implements the 64-bit RISC-V ISA (I, M, A, C, plus privilege
modes M/S/U on typical targets). It is also the anchor of a
build-platform-led SoC flow: one typed configuration file (.config.ts at the
repo root) parameterizes the core, the uncore (corev_apu), the board
(corev-mb), vendored controllers/PHY, foundry technology adaptation, and
optional structural timing analysis via sv-timing. Drive it with
g6lc-build (permanent alias: g6lc-build).The stack is intentionally opt-in and additive: the classic CVA6 core and
manual flow remain available; LibreCore extensions and tooling sit beside them
and are enabled only when you need them.This additive posture is critical for industrial adoption. A CPU IP block that
is forced to absorb board, tooling, or foundry concerns into its core
hierarchy quickly becomes unmaintainable; it accumulates ad hoc dependencies
that prevent reuse in other SoCs and make every tape-out a bespoke engineering
event. By keeping each layer optional, LibreCore preserves a clean, reusable
RISC-V implementation while surrounding it with a growing ecosystem of
integration tools. This is the same modularity principle that governs
commercial IP reuse programs, but expressed through open-source conventions:
configuration structs, file-system routing, and git-ignored drop-ins rather
than proprietary license managers and encrypted netlists.
data.how-this-documentation-is-organized#How:
The navigation on the left follows the same layers as the project:
Getting Started — install the toolchain and run your first checks.
Architecture & Worktree — a high-level map of every top-level directory and
how they connect.
CPU Core — pipeline, config, and product features (OoO, SMT, H, RVV).
Architecture — worktree, upgrade program,
SKU matrix.
corev_apu — uncore/FPGA layer, L2/L3, multi-core cluster.
corev-mb — the motherboard/board layer and SKiDL-based PCB design flow.
Technology / PDK — foundry adaptation with NDA-protected PDK drop-ins.
Build Platform — the g6lc-build command (probe, verify, timings, …).
sv-timing — standalone structural FO4 timing package and host adapter.
Guides — cross-cutting topics: agent workflows, building docs, and
AI-assisted development.
data.philosophy-general-before-specific#Philo:
Every page is written to age well as features are added. We avoid
hard-coding command output, exact line numbers, or one-off procedures. Instead,
each page describes the seam where a feature is added, the config gate that
controls it, the verification that validates it, and the agent guides that
explain it. When a new feature lands, the same structure still fits.The reason this level of abstraction endures is that the fundamental questions
of hardware engineering do not change with each feature. Whether the task is to
add a branch predictor, integrate a DDR controller, or bind a foundry memory
compiler, the same four questions must be answered: where is the seam, what
config gate controls it, how is it verified, and what contract does it expose
to software? By organizing every page around those four questions, we create
documentation that remains accurate even when file names change, line numbers
shift, and new subsystems appear. This is the difference between a procedure
list, which rots, and a design narrative, which compounds.
data.for-ai-agents-and-human-readers#For AI a:
The CVA6 repository contains a family of AGENTS-*.md files. They are
purpose-built for both humans and LLM agents: each guide states the intent of a
domain, the sanctioned seam for changes, and the exact checklist to satisfy
before a change is considered complete. Every section of this docs site maps to
those files and explains how an agent navigates them during a workflow.In practice, an agent is not replacing the engineer; it is amplifying the
engineer's ability to operate at the right level of abstraction. The AGENTS-*
files act as a curated retrieval layer, ensuring that an LLM loads only the
spec summaries, code loci, and checklists relevant to a given intent rather
than the entire repository. For a human reader, the same files provide a
reproducible review checklist. For an automated workflow, they provide a
planning contract. This dual use is what makes the CVA6 knowledge graph
different from a conventional wiki: it is written to be executed as well as
read.Start with Getting Started, or jump to the
worktree map if you want the big picture first.

This section contains cross-cutting guides that do not belong to a single layer
(core, APU, motherboard, etc.) but instead describe how the project is
developed and maintained.In a large hardware project, the most expensive mistakes are not technical
errors; they are process errors. A contributor may know how to write
SystemVerilog but not know which config struct to extend. An agent may know how
to fetch vendor IP but not know which license to record. Cross-cutting guides
exist to capture these process rules so that every task is performed in the
context of the project's architecture and governance.
data.pages#Pages:
Agent Workflow — how LLM agents navigate the CVA6
knowledge graph and AGENTS-* files.
Building the Docs — how this Next.js + Nextra site is
structured and extended.
Related layer docs (not under Guides but often next):
sv-timing — structural FO4 package
Build platform · Timings — monorepo host adapter
Probe, Diag & Verify — operator loop
data.why-cross-cutting-guides-matter#Why cros:
A hardware project has many moving parts: RTL, verification, board design,
vendor IP, foundry views, toolchain, and documentation. Without a shared
workflow, an agent or contributor has to re-discover the rules for every task.
The guides here encode the process so that the content in the other
sections can be applied correctly.The guides are the project's operating manual. They do not replace the deep
documentation in the AGENTS-*.md files or the technical details in the layer
sections; they explain how to move between those documents and how to decide
which one to read first. For an automated agent, they are the high-level
control flow; for a human, they are the onboarding and review checklist.

Auto-correct is an expert, opt-in path: measure on the IR → apply
scope-safe, allowlisted transforms → re-measure → emit rewritten SystemVerilog
plus an edit trace. It is not a silent rewriter of the monorepo tree.
data.safety-rules#Safety rules:
Allowlist / flags — destructive or latency-changing edits require
explicit consent (e.g. --allow-latency, module allowlists as implemented).
Never auto-commit — hosts must not merge emit trees into core/ without
human review.
Integrity — reparse + structural checks + fixture golden FO4; formal
functional equivalence of transforms is a non-goal for v1.
CVA6-style SV — emit follows project-oriented style notes in
sv-timing/architecture/CVA6-STYLE-SV.md when targeting similar RTL patterns.
data.optimization-surface--o#Optimization sur:
Presets map to a small set of dials (pipeline aggressiveness, operator
rewrites, area vs delay, etc.). Design delta:
sv-timing/architecture/OPTIMIZATION-LEVELS.md.Typical shape (names follow the package CLI; always check --help):
Level	Intent	-O0	Analyze / report only; minimal or no transform	-O1…-O2	Conservative structural improvements	-O3	Aggressive delay-oriented transforms (may add latency if allowed)	-Os / -Oz	Prefer fewer / smaller edits when closing is possible	
Exact dial maps live in sv-timing-core (opt.rs) and the design delta —
docs here deliberately avoid freezing bit-level dial IDs.

Transform ownership is split:

sv-timing/architecture/AUTO-CORRECT-CORE-API.md.

svt_corrected.f rather than in-place mutation of sources. See

data:
sv-timing/ is a project-independent Rust package that compiles an explicit
list of SystemVerilog sources into a timing-oriented intermediate
representation (IR), ranks combinational paths against a FO4-style budget and
a caller-supplied target frequency, and optionally applies allowlisted
auto-correct transforms that re-emit SystemVerilog with edit traces.It exists to give designers early, source-level structural feedback before
synthesis and static timing analysis (STA). Functionally correct RTL can still
be hostile to a high-frequency target; long combinational clouds, expensive
operators, and weakly explicit sequencing typically surface only after STA,
when restructuring is expensive.
Disclaimer: FO4 numbers and path ranks are structural estimates only.
They do not replace STA, SDF, place-and-route, or foundry sign-off. See
sv-timing/architecture/STA-HANDOFF.md for the handoff contract.
data.independence-hard-requirement#Independen:
The package builds, tests, and analyzes with only the sv-timing/ tree and
its fixtures. It has no compile- or link-time dependency on CVA6 RTL,
build-platform, monorepo flists, edaEnv, or SoC config packages.
Hosts (optional)                    Package (standalone)
─────────────────                   ────────────────────
flist / defines / MHz               parse → IR → FO4
param-map / cache path         →    path rank / report
spawn CLI / rehydrate JSON     ←    optional correct + emit
Hosts prepare inputs and consume outputs. They never pull monorepo code into
the crate graph. The CVA6 monorepo adapter is the build-platform timings
command; see Host Integration and
Build Platform · Timings.

From sv-timing/ (Python-first tooling under tools/):

data.timing-ir-conceptually#Timing IR (concep:
The IR is not a full elaborator netlist. It is a timing-oriented graph of:
Operators (add, mul, mux, compare, …) with FO4-class costs
Sequential elements and sequential/combinational region boundaries
Gating (clock edge, enable, reset) where recoverable from the source
Path endpoints (reg / port / hierarchical stitch)
Precise origins on every node for report anchors and edits
Expression trees (lhs_expr / rhs_expr) feed cost attribution and
synthesize/emit so rewrites can preserve recoverable RHS structure.
data.cost-model-and-frequency-budget#Cost mod:
Costs are structural FO4 estimates, calibrated from a package-owned table
(fo4-v1.toml), not process-corner cell libraries.
The caller supplies target frequency (--target-mhz; CLI default is
package-defined; CVA6 hosts often pass SoC targetFrequencyMHz, e.g. 1250).
Paths and regions are ranked against that budget so designers see
which source constructs threaten closure — not a P&R critical path.
Active measurement and optimization-surface deltas:
sv-timing/architecture/OPTIMIZATION-LEVELS.md.
data.cache#Cache:
Analyze results can hit a SQLite cache keyed by design inputs (file CRCs,
param-map, etc.). Cache path is caller-chosen (default under the working
directory). Throughput and a pre-compiled per-file units tier are described in
sv-timing/architecture/PERF-CACHE.md.Hosts should map cache and report directories into their own workspace (in CVA6:
under build-platform/workspace/) so package defaults do not pollute the RTL
tree.
data.portable-file-lists#Portable file lists:
The package understands a simple .f format: paths, comments, +incdir+,
+define+, nested -f/-F (cycle-guarded). Relative paths resolve against the
listing file’s directory.
Package-owned expand: python tools/svt.py flist --in entry.f --set VAR=…
Host-owned expand: Bender / FuseSoC / env-heavy EDA -F stay outside the
crates; hosts flatten to portable .f before analyze.
data.json-contract#JSON contract:
Analyze and correct emit versioned JSON (see sv-timing/schemas/). Hosts
rehydrate DTOs; they do not reimplement the cost model. The TypeScript client
under sv-timing/js/ documents the same shapes for Bun consumers.
data.sta-handoff#STA handoff:
Structural reports can produce hints (path comments, SDC-oriented notes)
for design review. Sign-off remains with the project’s STA flow and PDK
libraries. See sv-timing/architecture/STA-HANDOFF.md.

data:
The technology optimization pass adapts CVA6 to a specific foundry process by
binding proprietary high-level abstractions — memory compilers, ICG / retention
/ level-shifter cells, power kits, and hard macros — at the existing PDK-swap
seam. It is opt-in, additive, and macro-protected so the generic RTL path
remains byte-for-byte unchanged when the pass is not armed.Technology adaptation is the final bridge between functional RTL and
manufacturable silicon. A CPU core that simulates correctly with behavioral
models is not yet a chip; it must be mapped to a foundry's cells, memories,
clocking, and power network. The CVA6 technology pass performs this mapping
without forking the generic RTL, so the same source can be evaluated on
multiple process nodes and reused by partners who have access to different
foundries.
data.pdk-swap-seam#PDK-swap seam:
The seam is the set of technology-agnostic cells that a foundry can replace:
vendor/pulp-platform/tech_cells_generic/src/rtl/tc_sram.sv — SRAM macro
boundary.
vendor/pulp-platform/tech_cells_generic/src/rtl/tc_clk.sv — clock gating
(tc_clk_gating) and clock buffers.
vendor/pulp-platform/tech_cells_generic/src/rtl/tc_pwr.sv — power cells.
common/local/util/sram_cache.sv — TECHNO_CUT boundary.
HPDcache behav / blackbox / <tech> macros.
A foundry drop-in provides implementation views (.lib, .lef, .gds) and a
manifest.json under pd/pdk/<tech>/. The RTL wrapper lives under
pd/pdk/<tech>/<area>/ and is guarded by CVA6_TECH_OPT.
data.two-key-ignition#Two-key ignition:
The pass is inert by default. It arms only when both conditions are met:
technology.optimizationPass is true in .config.ts.
A *.tech-spec.md document exists under core/** or corev_apu/**
(governed by technology.specGlobs).
If either key is missing, the generic path builds exactly as before.
data.macro-protection#Macro protection:
Every adaptation is fenced behind the guard macro CVA6_TECH_OPT
(technology.guardMacro). When the macro is undefined, the generic path
elaborates. The `ifdef stays at the leaf; structure is still gated by
cva6_cfg_t.Example pattern:
`ifdef CVA6_TECH_OPT
  // foundry-specific tc_sram instantiation
`else
  // generic behavioral tc_sram
`endif
data.nda-protection#NDA protection:
Proprietary foundry content lives only under pd/pdk/, which is gitignored
by default. Only these files are committed:
pd/pdk/README.md, .gitignore, manifest.example.json
pd/pdk/core/README.md, .gitignore
pd/pdk/corev_apu/README.md, .gitignore
pd/pdk/technology.example/README.md, .gitignore
g6lc-build tech init <tech> scaffolds a gitignored per-tech drop-in. NDA
views (.lib, .lef, .gds, manifest.json) never enter the repository.The protected-path model is a legal and technical necessity. Foundry libraries
are proprietary and often covered by NDAs; committing them to a public
repository would violate license agreements and expose the project to legal
risk. At the same time, the build flow must know where to find these views
when the technology pass is armed. The pd/pdk/ scaffolding provides a stable,
predictable location while the .gitignore ensures that only READMEs and
templates are tracked.
data.commands#Commands:
g6lc-build tech status        # is the pass armed?
g6lc-build tech specs         # list discovered *.tech-spec.md docs
g6lc-build tech plan          # read-only adaptation plan
g6lc-build tech check         # hard + soft readiness gates
g6lc-build tech init <tech>   # scaffold a protected per-tech drop-in
tech check exits 3 when optimizationPass is on but a hard gate fails; it
exits 0 when the pass is disabled.
data.readiness-gates#Readiness gates:
Hard gates (must pass when armed):
Guard macro is a valid identifier.
pd/pdk/ root is gitignored.
Foundry PDK consistency (manifest or drop-ins present only when expected).
Soft gates (warned but not blocking):
requireExplicit — the user must explicitly enable the pass.
Readiness gates are the safeguards that prevent the technology pass from being
armed accidentally or with incomplete information. The guard-macro check
ensures that the ifdef in the RTL refers to a valid identifier. The
pd/pdk/ gitignore check ensures that proprietary content cannot be committed
by accident. The PDK consistency check ensures that the foundry views match the
configured technology. These gates are deliberately conservative because an
incorrect technology mapping can corrupt the netlist without failing
simulation.
data.soc-readiness#SoC-readiness:
An armed technology pass must still satisfy the same AGENTS.md §0 checklist as
any RTL change: synthesizability, verification, DFT, timing, power/UPF, area,
and documentation.The SoC-readiness checklist is not waived by the technology pass; if anything,
it is intensified. Foundry-specific cells have different timing arcs, power
characteristics, and test requirements than behavioral models. The pass must
therefore be followed by equivalence checking, DFT/MBIST verification, static
timing analysis, power intent validation, and area comparison. Only when the
optimized netlist passes the same functional and physical checks as the generic
netlist is the technology adaptation complete.See NDA Optimization Pass for the full agent workflow.

data:
This page is the practical workflow for binding a foundry's proprietary cells to
CVA6 while keeping the NDA content out of the repository.The technology optimization pass is the most sensitive workflow in CVA6
because it touches proprietary foundry information. It is designed to give
authorized users a controlled path to map the generic RTL to real silicon
without exposing that information in the open repository. The pass is therefore
opt-in, macro-protected, and gated by both a configuration flag and a
tech-spec document. This is the same class of controls used in commercial IP
flows to separate public RTL from proprietary process libraries.
data.when-to-use-this-pass#When to use this p:
Use the technology optimization pass when:
You have a signed NDA with a foundry and want to use their memory compiler,
standard-cell variants, retention cells, level shifters, power kits, or hard
macros.
You want to evaluate area, timing, and power on a specific process node.
You are preparing for tape-out and need the design to map to real PDK cells.
Do not use this pass for:
Generic behavioral simulation (it is inert by default).
Adding new ISA-visible features (use the core config + seams instead).
General refactoring of the RTL hierarchy.
The "do not use" list is as important as the "use" list. The technology pass
is not a general-purpose tool; it is a specific mechanism for technology
mapping. Using it for ISA-visible features or hierarchy refactoring would
contaminate the generic source with non-generic concerns and would violate the
separation of concerns that makes CVA6 reusable. The pass should be used only
when there is a real foundry library to bind and a real tape-out to prepare.
data.1-author-a-technology-spec-document#1. A:
Create a *.tech-spec.md under core/** or corev_apu/** that describes:
The target technology node and foundry.
Which cells are being replaced (SRAM, ICG, retention, level shifter, power,
hard macro).
The area(s) affected (core or corev_apu).
The expected synthesis / PnR / DFT impact.
Verification plan (equivalence, MBIST, timing, power, UPF).
This document is the second key that arms the pass.The tech-spec document is the reasoning artifact. It forces the engineer or
agent to state what is being replaced, why the replacement is necessary, and
how the change will be verified. This is essential for a workflow that can
silently change the netlist: without a written plan, it is impossible to
review whether the technology mapping is correct. The document also serves as a
record for future porting to other process nodes.
data.2-enable-the-pass-in-config#2. Enable th:
Edit .config.ts:
technology: {
  optimizationPass: true,
  pdkMode: 'nda',
  activeTechnology: 'demoTech',
  pdkRoot: 'pd/pdk',
  areaRoots: ['pd/pdk/core', 'pd/pdk/corev_apu'],
  specGlobs: ['core/**/*.tech-spec.md', 'corev_apu/**/*.tech-spec.md'],
  guardMacro: 'CVA6_TECH_OPT',
  protectedGlobs: ['pd/pdk/**'],
  requireExplicit: true,
}
Set pdkMode: 'omitted' or 'open' for public/open-source PDK experiments; set
'nda' only when you have an active foundry drop-in.
data.3-initialize-the-protected-drop-in#3. In:
g6lc-build tech init demoTech
This creates pd/pdk/demoTech/ with a README.md and .gitignore. Copy your
NDA views into this directory; they will be ignored by git.
data.4-plan-the-adaptation#4. Plan the adapta:
g6lc-build tech plan
The platform scans *.tech-spec.md files and the PDK drop-in, then prints a
read-only adaptation plan. It never edits RTL in this step.
data.6-wire-synthesis#6. Wire synthesis:
Pass +define+CVA6_TECH_OPT to the synthesis flow in pd/synth/Makefile or
through the build platform's physical-design integration. The foundry drop-in
must be on the include path for the target run.Synthesis is where the guard macro becomes real. When +define+CVA6_TECH_OPT
is passed, the synthesis tool sees the foundry wrapper and uses the proprietary
.lib and .lef views to size, place, and route the design. When the macro is
absent, the generic behavioral cells elaborate exactly as they did before. This
two-state behavior is the core of the technology pass: it is a single source
that can be elaborated generically or specifically depending on the target.
data.7-verify-soc-readiness#7. Verify SoC-rea:
Run g6lc-build tech check and then the standard verification flow:
Equivalence: generic vs optimized netlist.
DFT/MBIST: scan chains and memory BIST insertion.
Timing: STA on the target corner.
Power/UPF: power intent and rail analysis.
Area: compare against the generic mapping.
The verification list is what makes the technology pass more than a cell swap.
A foundry memory compiler may produce a smaller, faster SRAM, but it may also
introduce setup/hold violations, power-rail dependencies, or testability
requirements that the behavioral model did not have. Equivalence checking
ensures the netlist is functionally the same; DFT/MBIST ensures it is testable;
STA ensures it meets timing; UPF analysis ensures it can be powered correctly;
and area comparison ensures the optimization actually saved silicon. Each step
is a gate that prevents a silent regression.

data.agent-workflow-for-technology#Agent work:
An LLM agent asked to "optimize CVA6 for foundry X" should:
Read AGENTS-technology.md and
agents/guides/AGENTS-technology-optimization.md.
Confirm technology.optimizationPass and pdkMode in .config.ts.
Look for existing *.tech-spec.md or create one.
Run g6lc-build tech status and g6lc-build tech plan before any RTL edit.
Add guard-macro-protected wrappers at the PDK-swap seam.
Run g6lc-build tech check and synthesis equivalence checks.
Never commit foundry content; keep it under pd/pdk/<tech>/.
For an agent, the technology workflow is a test of discipline. The agent must
not edit the generic source, must not commit proprietary files, and must not
skip verification. The two-key ignition and the readiness gates exist precisely
to catch these mistakes before they reach the repository. A well-behaved agent
will read the tech-spec, run tech status, tech plan, and tech check, and
only then touch the guard-macro-protected wrappers.
data.common-agent-mistakes#Common agent mista:
Editing RTL without the guard macro. The generic path must remain
unchanged.
Committing NDA files. pd/pdk/ is gitignored for a reason.
Skipping the tech-spec document. The pass requires both keys.
Forgetting equivalence/DFT/timing. The technology pass is not a simple
cell swap; it is a SoC-readiness step.
These mistakes are the four fatal errors of technology adaptation. Editing RTL
without the guard macro forks the source and breaks the generic path.
Committing NDA files violates legal agreements and exposes the project.
Skipping the tech-spec removes the planning contract that makes the pass
reviewable. And skipping equivalence/DFT/timing produces a netlist that may
simulate but cannot be manufactured. The pass is designed to be safe only when
all four are respected.

The build platform in build-platform/ is a Bun + TypeScript project that
drives the entire CVA6 flow from a single typed config file (.config.ts). It
is the spine that connects the core, APU, motherboard, vendor IP, and
foundry/PDK adaptation.A build platform is more than a collection of scripts; it is the expression of
the project's workflow as a typed, versioned API. By centralizing the flow in a
single command, CVA6 ensures that every engineer and every automated agent
invokes the same logic, reads the same config, and reports the same exit codes.
This eliminates the "it worked on my machine" problem and makes CI, local
development, and agent execution interchangeable.

data.single-control-surface#Single control su:
The repo-root .config.ts is the only file a user normally needs to edit. It is
typed by build-platform/src/config/schema.ts, defaulted by
build-platform/src/config/defaults.ts, merged by
build-platform/src/config/load.ts, and validated before use.Example structure:
export default defineBuildConfig({
  soc: { coreConfig: 'cv64a6_imafdc_sv39' },
  tests: { defaultSuites: ['smoke-cv64a6'] },
  motherboard: { activeBoard: 'genesys2' },
  vendor: { controllers: [...] },
  technology: { optimizationPass: false },
})
Because the merge is DeepPartial, new options are automatically optional for
existing configs.The DeepPartial merge is a deliberate extensibility mechanism. It means that
adding a new config field does not require every existing user to update their
.config.ts; the default value is used unless overridden. This is how the build
platform can evolve without breaking the ecosystem. It also means that the
schema is the documentation: a contributor can read schema.ts and know every
available option and its type.

PlatformContext (src/context.ts) is the one object every command receives.
childEnv(ctx) builds the environment for CVA6 child processes (RISCV,
CVA6_REPO_DIR, VERILATOR_INSTALL_DIR, etc.).
src/workspace/discovery.ts provides file discovery and change detection.
data.zero-runtime-dependencies#Zero runtime d:
bun run works without bun install. Only devDependencies (type packages)
are used. All runtime code uses Bun/Web/Node built-ins. This keeps the platform
self-contained and fast to clone.Zero runtime dependencies are unusual for a TypeScript project, but they are a
major advantage for a hardware build platform. They eliminate the risk that a
package in node_modules will change behavior or disappear, and they allow the
platform to run from a fresh clone with only Bun installed. The platform uses
Bun's built-in APIs for file system, process spawning, and HTTP, which are fast
and stable. Type packages live in devDependencies for editor support and
tsc, but they never run in production.
data.contained-workspace#Contained workspace:
Everything the platform installs or produces goes under
build-platform/workspace/ (gitignored). Deletions are confined to that
directory. The repo outside workspace/ is never modified by normal commands.Containment is a trust property. Engineers and CI runners need to know that
running g6lc-build setup or g6lc-build clean will not delete their RTL,
their config, or their documentation. By confining all mutable state to a
gitignored workspace, the platform makes this guarantee explicit. This is
especially important for automated agents, which must be able to explore and
build without fear of corrupting the source tree.
data.cross-platform#Cross-platform:
No OS-specific assumptions outside src/platform/:
src/platform/os.ts — OS detection and conventions.
src/platform/exec.ts — Bun.spawn wrapper, which(), capture().
src/platform/shell.ts — pwsh/bash/zsh dispatch.
data.test-orchestration#Test orchestration:
The test command catalogues every non-vendored verif/regress/*.sh script.
Each suite has preflight checks: missing tool, missing submodule, or missing UVM
simulator causes the suite to be skipped with a reason, not failed. This
lets --open-source run cleanly without proprietary EDA.Preflight is the mechanism that makes the test suite portable. In a world where
some contributors have access to VCS, Questa, and UVM while others have only
Verilator and a laptop, the platform cannot simply fail when a tool is missing.
Instead, it reports a skip with a reason. This preserves the signal of the
tests that can run while being honest about the tests that cannot. It is the
difference between a red CI and an informative CI.
data.pages-in-this-section#Pages in this sect:
Probe, Diag & Verify — host readiness and §0.2 gate
Timings — sv-timing host adapter
Extending the Platform — add commands, config, tools, suites

The CVA6 build platform is designed so that new features are additive,
discovered automatically, and require touching as few files as possible. This
page is a concise recipe book.
data.add-a-configuration-option#Add a configu:
Add the typed field to build-platform/src/config/schema.ts.
Add its default value to build-platform/src/config/defaults.ts.
(Optional) Validate it in build-platform/src/config/load.ts.
Because the user config is a DeepPartial merged over defaults, the new option
is automatically optional for every existing .config.ts.The schema-first approach makes the build platform self-documenting. Every
config field has a type, a default, and a validation rule. When a new option is
added, the TypeScript compiler and the config loader immediately catch invalid
values. This is especially valuable for automated agents, which can read
schema.ts to discover the available control surface rather than guessing from
Makefiles or environment variables.
data.add-a-cli-command#Add a CLI command:
Create build-platform/src/cli/commands/<name>.ts exporting a Command
(name, summary, usage, needsContext, run).
Import it in build-platform/src/cli/registry.ts and append to COMMANDS.
Help text and dispatch pick it up automatically.The registry pattern is the plugin architecture of the build platform. It means
that adding a command does not require editing a central switch statement or
a command parser. Instead, the command exports a small object that the registry
discovers. This separation makes commands easy to test in isolation and easy
for an agent to add by following the same pattern.
data.add-a-managed-tool#Add a managed tool:
Add its install path to build-platform/src/tooling/locations.ts.
Add a version pin to schema.ts ToolVersions and defaults.ts.
Add a host probe to build-platform/src/tooling/detect.ts HOST_PROBES.
Add an installX recipe to build-platform/src/tooling/recipes.ts.
Wire it into build-platform/src/cli/commands/setup.ts and childEnv in
context.ts if it needs to be on the child PATH.
Managed tools are the platform's answer to the heterogeneous environments in
which CVA6 runs. A contributor on Windows may not have riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc
on their PATH; a CI runner may need a specific Verilator version; a laptop user
may prefer to use system packages. The platform probes the host, downloads or
builds the tool if allowed, and exposes it through childEnv. This gives every
command a consistent view of the toolchain while respecting the user's choice
to use system or managed tools.
data.add-a-regressiontest-suite#Add a regress:
Add a TestSuite entry to defaults.ts tests.suites (or .config.ts):
id, description, script, group, target, dvSimulators, tools
optional: dvTarget, testSuiteInstallers, requiresSubmodule,
requiresUvm, openSource, optional
Reference its id in tests.defaultSuites to include it in the default run.
test --list and bun test discover suites from config with no further code
change.The test suite catalog is config-driven. A new regression does not require a
new TypeScript command; it requires a new entry in the suite list. The runner
then preflights the suite, skips it if the environment is insufficient, and
reports the result. This model scales to dozens of suites because the code that
executes them is generic; only the metadata differs. It also makes it easy to
mark a suite as open-source, optional, or UVM-dependent without touching the
runner logic.
data.add-a-vendored-controller--phy#Add a ven:
Add a VendorControllerSpec to defaults.ts vendor.controllers or
.config.ts:
id, description, domain, kind, mechanism, url, path,
license, status, enabled, scanPaths, integrationSeam, phyNote,
architectureDoc
(Optional) Add a per-domain outline under architecture/uncore/.
g6lc-build vendor list|status|sync|add|update|scan discovers it automatically.The vendored controller catalog is the platform's extension point for uncore
IP. By describing a controller in config rather than committing its source, the
project keeps the repository free of stale or unlicensed copies while still
supporting a rich set of peripherals. The catalog metadata records where the IP
comes from, how it is integrated, and which PHY it requires. This is what
allows g6lc-build vendor sync to be reproducible and auditable.
data.add-a-motherboard#Add a motherboard:
Create corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json.
Write corev-mb/architecture/<id>/README.md and AGENTS-mb-<id>.md.
Run g6lc-build mb select <id>.
For custom boards, also use g6lc-build mb create <id> and the SKiDL flow.Adding a motherboard is the most cross-layer extension. It touches corev-mb/
for the board spec and contract, build-platform/src/tooling/motherboard.ts for
the generation logic, and potentially corev_apu/ for the APU wrapper. The
platform handles the common steps — validation, overlay writing, board package
generation — so the contributor can focus on the board-specific details. This
is the same additive philosophy: the core and APU are not edited, only
configured.
data.add-a-technology-optimization#Add a tech:
See NDA Optimization Pass. The build-platform
files to touch are:
build-platform/src/config/schema.ts — TechnologyConfig (already exists).
build-platform/src/config/defaults.ts — defaults (already exist).
build-platform/src/tooling/technology.ts — the engine.
build-platform/src/cli/commands/technology.ts — the tech command.
data.host-adapt-an-independent-package-worked:
Some tools must stay project-independent (no monorepo imports in their
crates). Integrate them the same way timings integrates sv-timing/:
Keep the package under its own root with its own tests and AGENTS.
Add host helpers under build-platform/src/tooling/<name>.ts that:
expand project manifests (flists, env) into package-portable inputs;
build argv / env;
spawn the package CLI (never link monorepo modules into the package).
Add src/cli/commands/<name>.ts + register it in registry.ts.
Document the boundary in the package’s host guide and on this site
(Timings, sv-timing host integration).
Do not put CVA6 paths, ariane_pkg, or edaEnv into the independent package’s
compile graph.
data.validation-after-changes#Validation afte:
cd build-platform
bun install            # once, for dev type packages
bunx tsc --noEmit      # strict type-check
bun test               # fast unit tests (+ skipped regression specs)
bun run src/cli/index.ts doctor
bun run needs no install; tsc and editor types do.The validation sequence is the safety net for platform changes. Type-checking
catches schema and command signature errors before runtime. The unit tests
verify config loading, suite discovery, and command dispatch. The doctor
command confirms that the host environment is still healthy. Running these
three commands after any platform change is the minimum due diligence; without
them, a small TypeScript error can propagate into the whole build flow.

The core/ directory contains the CVA6 RISC-V CPU. It is designed to be
compiled, simulated, and synthesized stand-alone. It has no dependency on the
APU, the board layer, or the build platform.This independence is the foundation of CVA6's industrial value. In a commercial
IP flow, the CPU core is often licensed separately from the SoC integration
layer; it must compile in environments where the board, peripherals, and
foundry libraries are not yet known. By ensuring that core/ has no
dependency on the outer layers, CVA6 can be integrated into many SoCs without
forcing each integrator to adopt a specific tool chain or board definition. The
core is where the RISC-V architecture is realized; everything else is context.
data.what-the-core-implements#What the core i:
ISA: 64-bit RISC-V I, M, A, C with privilege modes M, S, U (extensions
grow with package: H, Sstc, RVB, Zicbo*, optional RVV, …).
Pipeline: 6-stage baseline; config-gated multi-issue, slice-OoO, and
full OoO (OoOEn) on production packages.
Threads: optional SMT2 (NrHarts=2) with banked arch state.
Memory: TLBs, hardware PTW, configurable L1; L2/L3 attach on the APU
side when enabled.
Branch prediction: BTB/BHT/RAS plus upgraded prediction fabric / FTQ on
primary targets.
Observability: RVFI probes, debug triggers, PMU counters (including OoO
and cache hierarchy groups where wired).
The same RTL elaborates as a minimal embedded core, a Linux-capable application
core, an OoO server package, or an SMT bring-up target by selecting the right
config package. That is the product model — not separate forks.
data.product-level-pages#Product-level pages: Topic	Page	Roadmap / U1–U10 map	Upgrade Program	Package comparison	SKU Matrix	Prediction / FTQ	Frontend Extensions	Issue width	Multi-Issue	Rename / IQ / ROB / LSQ	Out-of-Order	Dual hardware threads	SMT	H + Sstc	Hypervisor & Sstc	RVV / Ara	Vector (RVV) & Ara	Named server packages	Server Profiles	L2/L3 (APU)	L2 / L3 Cache	Multi-core cluster	Multi-Core Cluster
data.how-to-read-the-core#How to read the cor:
The core is organized by pipeline stage and subsystem:
Area	Subdirectory / file	Responsibility	Fetch	frontend/	Prediction fabric, FTQ, instruction queue	Decode / Issue	issue_stage.sv, issue_read_operands.sv	Scoreboard, operand read, multi-issue	Slice / full OoO	cva6_slice_*.sv, ooo/	Slice path / rename·IQ·ROB·LSQ (gated)	SMT	smt/	Thread select, banked RF/PC/CSR	Execute	ex_stage.sv	ALU, FPU, multiplier, divider, branch unit, CSR, CVXIF	Load / Store	load_store_unit.sv, load_unit.sv, store_unit.sv, store_buffer.sv	Memory access, ordering, MMU interaction	Commit	commit_stage.sv, controller.sv	Retire, exception/flush, redirect	Caches / MMU	cache_subsystem/, cva6_mmu/, pmp/	L1, PTW, TLB, PMP
data.the-config-struct-is-the-gate#The config:
config_pkg::cva6_cfg_t (defined in core/include/config_pkg.sv) is the single
source of truth for feature selection. A feature is enabled by extending the
struct and the per-target config packages (core/include/cv64a6_*_config_pkg.sv,
core/include/cv32a6_*_config_pkg.sv), not by editing modules ad hoc.Key config domains:
cache_type_t / DCacheType — D$ subsystem selection.
bp_type_t / BPType / BTBEntries / BHTEntries / RASDepth — branch
predictor.
vm_mode_t — virtual-memory mode (Sv32, Sv39, Sv48, Sv57).
Axi*Width — memory-side bus width.
InstrTlbEntries / DataTlbEntries — TLB sizing.
NrScoreboardEntries / NrLoadBufEntries / MaxOutstandingStores —
speculation / in-flight window.
NrIssuePorts / SuperscalarEn — multi-issue width.
OoOEn / SliceOoOEn — full vs slice out-of-order (mutually exclusive).
NrHarts / SMT policy fields — simultaneous multithreading.
(APU-side) L2En / L3En / prefetch — not L1 fields; see L2/L3 page.
check_cfg(...) assertions enforce legality (power-of-two geometry, region-rule
counts, OoO/SMT legality, etc.).check_cfg is the contract enforcer. It encodes the architectural and
microarchitectural invariants that the RTL assumes. For example, if a cache
geometry is not a power of two, the indexing logic will silently produce
incorrect results; if the RAS depth is zero, the return-address stack will
misbehave. By expressing these as assertions in the config package, CVA6 turns
configuration errors from runtime mysteries into elaboration-time failures. This
is especially important when an agent or a new contributor extends the struct:
the assertions teach the valid design space.
data.development-guidelines#Development guide:
Spec-anchored. An ISA-visible change must start with the spec anchor in
specs/riscv-spec.html and update AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md.
Config-gated. Extend cva6_cfg_t and the target packages before touching
modules.
Synth-clean. Use always_ff / always_comb; no simulation-only
constructs in the logic path; respect the async-active-low reset strategy.
Backend-friendly. Memories go through tc_sram; clock gating through
tc_clk_gating; power cells through tc_pwr.
Observable. Add RVFI probes, PMU events, and debug trigger visibility.
Verified. Add a directed test and keep the compliance regression green.
Ecosystem-safe. The feature must be discoverable (misa/ISA string) and
toolchain/SBI/Linux-visible.
Each guideline addresses a failure mode that is expensive to fix late in the
design cycle. Spec-anchoring prevents subtle ISA incompatibilities. Config
gating prevents one target from breaking another. Synth-clean code ensures
that a change that simulates can also be fabricated. Backend-friendly cells
ensure that synthesis and place-and-route flows can target multiple processes.
Observability ensures that post-silicon debug is possible. Verification parity
prevents regression. And ecosystem safety ensures that the feature is usable by
the broader software stack, which is the ultimate customer of the RTL.
data.sanctioned-seams-for-new-features#Sancti:
New instructions — prefer the CVXIF coprocessor boundary (core/cvxif_fu.sv,
core/acc_dispatcher.sv).
New cache policy / L1 geometry — extend cva6_cfg_t and select in
core/cva6.sv.
New branch predictor — extend bp_type_t and implement in
core/frontend/.
New memory/TLB feature — extend vm_mode_t or TLB parameters and the MMU
in core/cva6_mmu/.
These seams are not arbitrary boundaries; they are the points where the RTL
structure naturally accepts variation. The CVXIF coprocessor interface exists
precisely because custom accelerators should not perturb the in-order pipeline.
The cache selection in core/cva6.sv exists because cache subsystem design is
a target-specific decision. The branch-predictor enum exists because predictor
choice is a classic area/timing/accuracy trade-off. By routing all feature
additions through these seams, CVA6 preserves the integrity of the pipeline
while allowing rich configurability.
data.agent-workflow-for-core-work#Agent workf:
Open AGENTS.md and find the intent row (branch prediction, RAM, L2/L3,
speculation, etc.).
Read the linked agents/guides/AGENTS-*.md and agents/spec/*.html.
Plan the config change, the code seam, and the verification.
Run g6lc-build test --open-source or the relevant arch group.
Update AGENTS-specs-to-impl.md, AGENTS-specs-to-tests.md, and
AGENTS-dts-validation.md if needed.
See CPU Architecture Guidelines for a deeper look at the
development patterns.

SKiDL is a Python library that lets you describe schematics in code. In
corev-mb/, it is the design-language for custom boards. It is not a board
id; it is the PCB counterpart to AGENTS-coding-philosophy.md.PCB design has historically lagged software in version control and automation.
Schematics are often binary or proprietary-format files that cannot be diffed,
parametrized, or reviewed in the same way as source code. SKiDL changes this by
representing the schematic as a Python program. In the CVA6 flow, this program
is generated from board.json, fed with real part data, and checked by ERC.
The result is a board design that is as reproducible and reviewable as the
SystemVerilog that runs on the die.
data.why-skidl#Why SKiDL:
Version-controllable. Schematics are text, not binary files.
Parametric. Reuse a board template for multiple SoC configs.
Programmable. Parts, nets, and ERC rules can be generated from
board.json or fetched from pcbparts.dev.
Lintable. The same Python tooling that checks the build can check the
schematic.
data.where-it-lives#Where it lives:
corev-mb/lib/ contains the Python support:
pcbparts_mcp.py — stdlib MCP client for pcbparts.dev (14 tools for part
search, stock check, pinouts, alternatives, board search, design rules, etc.).
soc.py — build_board() that translates a board.json into a SKiDL netlist.
interfaces.py — lazy SKiDL interfaces for common SoC/PHY connections.
erc.py — electrical-rule checks and the ERC loop.
The Python library in corev-mb/lib/ is intentionally small and uses the
standard library for the MCP client, so it does not introduce a heavy dependency
chain. SKiDL itself is the only non-stdlib package required, and it is treated
as a design-time tool, not a runtime dependency. This keeps the board layer as
light and portable as the other layers.
data.the-design-loop#The design loop:
board.json
    ↓
g6lc-build mb design <id> [--online]
    ↓
  soc.py builds the SKiDL skeleton from board.json
  interfaces.py adds SoC/PHY nets
  pcbparts_mcp.py selects concrete parts (online = live, offline = stub/cache)
  erc.py checks nets, power rails, pin mappings
    ↓
generated netlist / BOM / placement hints
    ↓
g6lc-build mb expand <id>   # generate KiCad/netlist/positions
g6lc-build mb test <id>     # rerun ERC and report
The loop is a closed design-verification cycle. board.json specifies intent;
soc.py and interfaces.py translate intent into a netlist; pcbparts_mcp.py
selects real components; and erc.py validates the result. Each iteration
can tighten the design without redrawing schematics by hand. This is the same
continuous-integration pattern used in software, but applied to hardware
connectivity.
data.part-selection-with-pcbpartsdev#Part sel:
The pcbparts MCP client is cache-first. By default it returns stubs from a
local cache so the design flow works offline. With --online, it queries the
pcbparts.dev MCP server over HTTP JSON-RPC/SSE.Cache-first operation is a deliberate design for hardware design workflows.
Hardware engineers often work in secure environments or on laptops without
reliable internet access. A cache-first client ensures that the SKiDL loop can
run offline, using the last-known part data and stub responses. The --online
flag then provides an explicit opt-in to live data, which is appropriate when
querying stock levels, prices, or the latest pinouts.Typical tools used:
jlc_search — find passives, connectors, and common ICs.
jlc_get_part / jlc_get_pinout — confirm footprint and pinout.
mouser_get_part / digikey_get_part — alternatives.
get_design_rules — board-house constraints.
data.power-rail-planning#Power-rail planning:
A board is a network of power domains. The SKiDL process explicitly plans:
SoC core / IO / PLL / DDR rails.
PHY rail requirements (e.g. RGMII IOVDD, DDR VREF).
Regulator and decoupling placement.
ERC checks for shorts, missing connections, and level mismatches.
data.soc-pin--phy-mapping#SoC-pin ↔ PHY mappi:
interfaces.py translates logical interfaces from board.json into physical
nets:
# pseudo-code
for iface in board['interfaces']:
    for pin in iface['pins']:
        soc_pin = soc[pin['soc']]
        phy_pin = phy[pin['phy']]
        soc_pin += phy_pin
The mapping is checked by erc.py for:
Pin function match (input to output, bidirectional to bidirectional).
Voltage level compatibility.
Pull-up/down and termination.
Differential-pair completeness.
The pin-mapping check is where most board design errors are caught. A missing
connection, a reversed differential pair, or a 1.8 V signal routed to a 3.3 V
pin will pass a visual review but fail ERC. By encoding the mapping rules in
Python, the SKiDL process makes these checks repeatable and exhaustive. This is
especially valuable for complex SoC packages with hundreds of pins, where
manual checking is error-prone.
data.physical-positioning-and-layout-intent#P:
SKiDL itself does not produce a PCB layout, but g6lc-build mb expand can
generate placement hints (e.g. group PHYs near the SoC edge, keep DDR traces
short and matched, place decoupling capacitors close to power pins). These hints
feed the board house's layout tool.Layout intent is the bridge between circuit design and mechanical design. SKiDL
does not draw the board, but it can express constraints that the layout tool
should honor: group high-speed PHYs near the SoC, keep DDR traces matched in
length, place power regulators near their loads, and put decoupling capacitors
close to power pins. These constraints are captured in code, so they travel
with the design and can be validated against the final layout.
data.agent-workflow-for-custom-boards#Agent w:
Read AGENTS-mb-skidl.md and AGENTS-motherboard.md.
Run g6lc-build mb create <id> to scaffold board.json and a starter
design.py.
Edit corev-mb/boards/<id>/board.json and corev-mb/architecture/<id>/README.md.
Run g6lc-build mb design <id> [--online] for the SKiDL loop.
Iterate on ERC errors with g6lc-build mb design <id> --fix.
Generate outputs with g6lc-build mb expand <id>.
Validate with g6lc-build mb test <id>.
The agent workflow for custom boards is a synthesis of the board specification
and the design automation loop. The agent starts with the governance documents,
creates a JSON spec, and then iterates on the SKiDL netlist until ERC passes.
The final outputs — netlist, BOM, and placement hints — are the deliverables
that a board house needs to produce a PCB. This workflow makes a custom board as
reproducible as a software build.
data.when-not-to-use-skidl#When not to use SK:
Reference or third-party boards set "skidl": "omitted". They ship a
manually-created schematic and layout; corev-mb/ only stores the board JSON
and contract. The genesys2 reference board is in this category.SKiDL is a tool for new board designs, not a mandate for all boards. Reference
and third-party boards often have existing schematics, layouts, and
manufacturing relationships that predate the CVA6 flow. In those cases, the
JSON contract and per-board AGENTS-mb-<id>.md document are sufficient. The
build platform can still select and configure these boards without running the
SKiDL loop.

This documentation site is a Next.js + Nextra project under
docs/website/. It uses file-based routing: every .mdx file in pages/
becomes a page automatically.Documentation is a first-class build artifact in CVA6. It is not an
afterthought appended to a release; it is part of the repository and is built,
versioned, and deployed with the same care as the RTL. Treating docs as code
means they can be reviewed in diffs, validated by automated tools, and extended
by agents using the same workflow as source code. The docs/website/ site is
the modern, interactive complement to the existing Sphinx manuals.
data.why-nextra#Why Nextra:
After reviewing Fumadocs, Mintlify, Docusaurus, and custom MDX loaders, Nextra
was chosen because it provides the fastest path to a polished, content-first
Next.js docs site with:
File-system routing and auto-generated sidebars.
MDX-first content.
Built-in full-text search, dark/light mode, and copy-to-code buttons.
Minimal configuration for standard documentation sites.
Fumadocs is a strong alternative for teams that want a more composable,
product-integrated docs shell; Nextra is the better fit for a lightweight,
content-heavy guide that can grow one Markdown file at a time.The choice of Nextra over alternatives reflects the project's values. Fumadocs
and Mintlify are strong for product-integrated docs, but they often assume a
dedicated docs team and a managed hosting environment. Docusaurus is powerful
but heavier in configuration and plugin management. Nextra provides the right
balance for CVA6: it is built on Next.js, so it integrates with the same
ecosystem as the build platform; it supports MDX natively, so technical content
can embed components and code; and it generates static HTML, so it can be
hosted anywhere without vendor lock-in.
data.directory-layout#Directory layout:
docs/website/
  next.config.mjs         # Nextra + static export config
  theme.config.tsx        # Nextra theme settings
  tsconfig.json           # TypeScript config
  package.json            # Next.js + Nextra dependencies
  pages/                  # Content (file-based routing)
    _app.tsx              # Global app wrapper + theme CSS
    _meta.ts              # Top-level sidebar order
    index.mdx             # /
    getting-started.mdx   # /getting-started
    architecture/         # /architecture/*
    core/                 # /core/*
    corev-apu/            # /corev-apu/*
    corev-mb/             # /corev-mb/*
    technology/           # /technology/*
    build-platform/       # /build-platform/*
    sv-timing/            # /sv-timing/*
    guides/               # /guides/*
  public/                 # Static assets
  dist/                   # Static export output (gitignored)
The directory layout is deliberately simple. pages/ is the content; _meta.ts
files control the sidebar; theme.config.tsx controls the appearance; and
next.config.mjs controls the static export. This simplicity is important for
an open-source hardware project where contributors may be more familiar with
SystemVerilog than with TypeScript. The docs site should be easy to extend
without becoming a frontend project in its own right.Do not add empty placeholder directories under pages/ for “future” sections —
real content lives in top-level sections (build-platform/, sv-timing/,
core/, …). Nested empty dirs only confuse the file tree.
data.adding-a-page#Adding a page:
Create a .mdx file under docs/website/pages/<section>/.
Add frontmatter:
---
title: Page Title
description: Short description.
---
Add the file name to the section's _meta.ts for sidebar ordering.
If no _meta.ts entry is added, Nextra will still show the page, but with a
derived title and default order.Adding a page is a three-step process: write the content, add frontmatter, and
register the page in the section's _meta.ts. The registration step is what
gives the page its place in the sidebar and its discoverability. Because Nextra
uses file-system routing, a page can exist without registration, but it will be
harder to find. This small ceremony ensures that new content is intentionally
placed in the information architecture.
data.adding-a-section#Adding a section:
Create a directory under pages/.
Add an index.mdx for the section landing page.
Add a _meta.ts for the section's sidebar.
Add the section name to pages/_meta.ts.
Adding a section follows the same pattern as adding a page, but at the
directory level. A section needs an index.mdx landing page, a _meta.ts for
its own sidebar, and an entry in the top-level _meta.ts. This hierarchical
structure maps directly to the layered architecture of CVA6, so readers can
navigate from the top-level concepts down to the specific layer or workflow
they need.
data.local-development#Local development:
./docs.sh dev
Or directly:
cd docs/website

data.static-build#Static build:
./docs.sh build
The output is written to docs/website/dist. You can serve it with any static
host (Vercel, GitHub Pages, Netlify, an internal nginx server, etc.).The static export is what makes the docs site portable. It does not require a
Node.js server at runtime; it is a collection of HTML files and assets that can
be served by any web server. This is ideal for open-source projects that may be
hosted on GitHub Pages, mirrored internally, or shipped as offline
documentation with a release. The build command ./docs.sh build wraps the
Next.js export in a consistent, cross-platform interface.
data.linking-between-pages#Linking between pa:
Use relative Markdown links:
See [CPU Architecture](../core/cpu-architecture).
Nextra resolves these automatically.Relative links are the correct way to reference other pages in the docs. They
keep the link graph local to the content and make the site robust to changes in
base URL or hosting path. Absolute paths or external URLs should be used only
when pointing outside the docs site. This discipline is especially important
for a static export, where URL structure is determined at build time.
data.writing-style#Writing style:
General before specific. Avoid exact line numbers, command output, or
version pins unless necessary.
Seam-first. Describe where a feature is added, how it is gated, and how
it is verified.
Agent-readable. Use explicit file paths and command names so an LLM can
follow the instructions.
Cross-reference. Link to the relevant AGENTS-*.md files and build
platform commands.
The writing style is designed for a dual audience: human engineers who need to
understand the project, and automated agents who need to execute instructions.
"General before specific" keeps the content stable as the code evolves. "Seam-first" aligns the explanation with the project's architecture. "Agent-readable"
ensures that file paths and commands are explicit enough to be parsed. And
"Cross-reference" ties every page back to the authoritative guides and the
build platform. A page that follows these rules will remain useful as the
project grows.
